If it passes through an aperture smaller than it's wavelength it bends and it's as if the aperture is it's origin. They will build up the wave pattern that would have existed if you had released them all at once or released a wave.  Why does it feel like light travels in a straight line?  It's because things are clear and precise.  But keep in mind the only thing that has to be straight is the wave front.  It's the straight wave front that is projected onto your retina. Author: @segevstormlord3713
Content:
THe issue I tend to take with this - and I am not (unusually enough for dealing with quantum mechanics) saying this is _wrong_ because of my issue - is that the apocryphal Feynman story stops short of something: why did the electron in the infinite-slit experiment wind up...anywhere? We always talk about "observation" as causing a "collapse of the wave function" and that imposes position and velocity definition upon the quantum-scale particle. But "observation" is just one of the things that creates the collapse condition: it is _interaction_ that causes collapse (and that interaction is a necessary part of observation, which is why "observation" is brought up so much). 

So, what we really have is a "probability of interaction" with all possible other entities existing in the same universe. And, because these ARE probabilities, just as with quantum tunneling, there must exist a non-zero probability that the particle "took" any given path... and that means it might well show up in a highly-improbable place.

And what governs macro-scale interactions - such as planets orbiting the sun - are the fact that all of those entities moving together as "a planet" are interacting with each other so very, very often that they "collapse the waveform" practically constantly, leading to "most likely" movement from interaction to interaction being resolved near-constantly, forcing even the rare occurences of non-standard Action to be overwhelmed by the massively more common least-Action moves.

Now, though, does this mean that, in an otherwise empty universe with a source of a single particle and a single detector, the single detector will _always, eventually_ detect the particle, since even though the probability of any given path to it is very very small, there is no other thing for it to interact with, so only those paths which have interaction with the detector can possibly happen in finite time?

Author: @subatomike
Content: I'm thinking the last laser experiment might be more tricky, and maybe needs some more care. Most of the discussion about action with multi-slit screens assumes an infinite plane wave is incident on the slits. In that case it makes sense that the resulting pattern on the detector screen will require adding the amplitudes (and squaring) at all possible slits. But if you illuminate with a laser, you have another amplitude to contend with, which is the amplitude of a spatial Gaussian mode from the laser. That amplitude approaches zero as you go further away from the beam's average k-vector (as defined by the laser cavity), which means the amplitude at each slit gets MULTIPLIED by the Gaussian mode. That means slits that are far away have negligible contribution instead of the equal weighted sum from the plane wave example. This is why I say more care might be needed in the laser experiment: You might have been seeing scatter from the end of the laser pointer instead of the tail of the Gaussian mode. BTW, the comment in the previous experiment using the bulb, that "it's just a diffraction grating" is the whole point! A diffraction grating is exactly what Feynman meant... diffraction gratings are a perfect example of photons exploring all possible paths!

Author: @sigma-signifier
Content:
If you have an infinite series of slits, you also have an infinite series of walls, meaning obstacles, which would nullify all the infinite slits, as they would block all possible paths where the photons can go, meaning there would be no interference at all.

Instead of passing through all possible trajectories at once, at infinite points in space, I think it's clear that there is only ever one outcome. And if there is only ever one outcome, then a photon clearly does not take all paths possible. It CAN take all paths possible, but it never does. It only ever takes one path. And it only ever goes through one slit, and or it hits the wall, and is absorbed or reflected before ever going through the slit. You can use math to describe the vector of a photon, but you can't observe or measure the vector, because it goes too fast to observe or to measure it. But the equation of the vector is not in itself the path of the physical vector that the photon has traveled. You can observe a light beam, but it is not the vector of one photon, it is the vector of many combined in a harmonic resonance. You're seeing the entire amplitude, wavelength, frequency of many photons at the same time, which all points to one direction. They are not pointing in all directions at once are they? A light beam does not light up an entire room does it? That is proof enough to say that light doesn't travel in all possible directions at once. I don't get the logic of this video at all. There are some interesting points though, that light enters a medium at a specific angle of the shortest path possible. I did not know it did that, and as such, I learned something new. But as for the conclusion that light travels all possible paths, and what is said about the double-slit experiment is simply not true. Those are probabilistic assumptions about a physical outcome. Interference patterns are not probabilistic no matter how you look at them. 

In other words, the MATH explores all possible paths. The calculations explores all possible paths. Quantum mechanics explores all possible paths. The photon never does. It only ever follows one path. And you can say that for any ACTION. 

You can think all possible thoughts, but you can only ever act on one of them. You have an almost endless choices and options to choose from, but you can only ever make once choice. There are literally millions of ways for you to live and die, but the history, or the trajectory of your life only ever follows one path, and you can only ever die once. Unless, of course, the universe is infinite... or the cycle of a finite universe is infinite, in which case you can be born again in another cycle that is configured exactly the same. However, it's not the same cycle, even though it has the exact same configuration.

And if you say: "Well in his experiment at the end, the light did as he said it would!" NO! That is not what is going on. He did not send ONE photon with the potential of going in any possible directions. He turned on a light BULB (spherical object) sending out photons in an omnidirectional pattern, illuminating the entire room. That is not one single photon. That is 8.3x10^18 times photons per second! So, of course you will see photons following every single path in the room when they are physically following every single path in the room! It's like a... *palm to the face* type of moment of sheer disbelief on my part. They've done all this research, but they're making obvious dumb assumptions.

And if you say: "Well, he did the same with a laser". Well, yes, a laser also emits the same amount of photons, except it isn't in an omnidirectional path, but sort of the same path. However, there is still NOT ONE photon being emitted, there are just as many photons emitted from the laser as the bulb, just in a more directional path. But if you actually look at the laser pen that he is using, it has a bulb too. It is emitting in an omnidirectional way. There is spillage of light from the bulb at the end of the laser pen, it's just fainter than the directed light of the focused beam, since the laser pen is blocking and directing most of the photons in seemingly the same direction, but not actually in the same direction. The bulb in the pen is spherical and omnidirectional. It's just blocked by the tube of the pen and focused into a funnel emitted as a seemingly straight line. This doesn't prove that light is going in all possible paths inside the room. It just shows that the pen he is using emits light in an omnidirectional way, just like the larger bulb he used, but fainter and more directional than the larger bulb from the lamp. The red light we see reflected in the mirror from the laser is spillage from the pen.

Is mathematics a human invention that we discovered describes nature, or is it the fundamental language of the universe that we gradually discover?

 Predict new phenomena (like the positron)
 Provide incredibly accurate models (like the electron's magnetic moment)
 Open technological horizons (lasers, transistors, quantum computers)

Perhaps the answer lies midway: we invent mathematical tools that reflect our limited insight into reality, then we discover that these very tools reveal deeper layers of truth, which in turn inspire new mathematical tools.

It's a dance between the human mind and the universe, where we create tools to understand reality, and then reality itself conforms to these tools in ways that exceed our expectations

Author: @ÇizilmişGİBİ
Content:
My Concern Regarding the Perfection of the Laser in the Veritasium Experiment (30:25)
I am referring to the second part of the final demonstration (around 30:25) where the laser light is shone onto the diffraction grating and light is observed reflecting from areas that should theoretically be dark, thus demonstrating Feynman's Path Integral formulation and the constructive interference of "crazy paths."
My concern revolves around the imperfection of the laser source. While a laser is generally considered highly collimated (directional), it is not perfectly so. Even when a laser beam is aimed away from an observer at an angle (say, 30° or 45°), one can often still see a faint glow or a scattering of light near the aperture or lens. This is due to various forms of classical scattering (e.g., reflections off the lens surface, imperfections in the laser assembly, or Rayleigh scattering).
This scattering means that even when the main beam is not aimed at the foil, some stray light is already "sprayed" in directions that are not along the predicted classical path.
For the experiment to be a truly compelling demonstration of quantum mechanics (where the diffraction grating selects for paths that would otherwise destructively interfere), all possibility of classical stray light hitting the grating and then being diffracted must be eliminated.
The Critique:
If we can see the laser working just by looking at its tip at a wide angle (like 30° or 45°), it suggests that scattered light is already traveling towards the foil from an angle before it hits the grating. The light we see in the dark regions of the reflection pattern might just be this pre-scattered light being conventionally diffracted by the foil, rather than the quantum phenomenon of the "straight-path" light exploring all possibilities.
My Suggestion for Improvement:
To ensure the validity of the demonstration, the laser must be made as close to a "perfect" directional source as possible:
• Collimation Tube: An extension tube or cylinder could be added to the end of the laser.
• Light-Absorbing Interior: The inside of this cylinder should be coated with a highly light-absorbing material (like Vantablack or flocking material) to trap and eliminate any stray light reflecting off the lens or housing.
If an observer were to look at the laser aperture from an angle (say, 30°), they should not be able to tell if the laser is on or off (i.e., no detectable light should escape). If, under these perfected conditions, the foil still produces reflections from the "dark" region, it would serve as much stronger evidence for the quantum mechanical concept of a particle truly exploring all possible paths.
Thank you for such an insightful video and allowing for this discussion.

First: If mathematics is discovered

Then we assume that numbers, ratios, and equations have always existed in the universe — we merely uncover them, just as we uncover the laws of physics.
This idea is championed by the Mathematical Platonists, who believe that mathematics is the language of the universe itself, not a human invention.

From their point of view, patterns like the golden ratio, Fibonacci sequence, or geometric symmetry in crystals were there long before we ever thought of them.
In a sense, the universe thinks mathematically.
Even Einstein leaned toward this view when he said:

In the structure of reality itself?

In this view, humans created mathematics as a tool for reasoning and description,
just as we created language, logic, and law.

Mathematics is not an absolute truth, but a symbolic system — a way to connect observations to predictions.

---

⚛️ Third: Between discovery and invention

Many modern thinkers believe the truth lies somewhere in between.
Mathematics is neither a pure invention nor a pure discovery —
it is a negotiated language between our minds and the universe’s structure.

It works because it captures some aspects of reality,
but it remains insufficient to fully contain it.

That’s why, whenever we approach the edges of knowledge — such as black holes, quantum mechanics, or the origin of the universe — mathematics itself starts to break down or contradict itself.
This strongly suggests that our mathematical framework is an approximation of reality, not its mirror.

Author: @jonathanrobertson7059
Content:
29:50 you can see that the laser pointer is not perfect; it's emitting light in all directions. Otherwise the only way you would see light from the laser pointer is if it's reflecting directly off the mirror into the camera; there would only be one dot, and it would line up directly with the laser pointer.
I personally believe that this small amount of global illumination is what the camera is picking up through directional refraction/reflection on the foil.
For a more accurate experiment, to mitigate the global illumination from the laser pointer, point it through a skinny tube of black construction paper to absorb the scattered light so you're left with a singular beam of directional light. If you get an actual true laser pointer with no stray light casting out in all directions and the dots still show up then you'd have me convinced, but as it stands, that reflection off the foil is clearly due to the fact that light is reflected at different angles by the foil. I think it's having the same effect that placing several reflective balls on top of the mirror would have: each ball would have an illuminated dot on it because there is a point on each ball that will result in an angle of reflection that intersects with the camera. Instead of several balls you just have a material that cycles through different reflective angles so global illumination will result in light reflecting to the camera at those specific points.

Content:
Hi Derek,

The idea that a photon “takes all possible paths” works mathematically, but it fails physically. A photon is real energy — a wave — not just a formula.

If it literally took all paths at once, its energy would add up across all trajectories, creating absurd spacetime effects, potentially even a black hole.

We need a framework where the particle follows a single definite path, guided by a weak energy wave, consistent with real energy and curvature. This explains observed patterns without invoking multiple universes or impossible gravitational effects.

The standard method predicts outcomes but does not describe what actually happens. A physically grounded theory is needed.

Best,
Johan Runegrund

Pretty sure that the demo at 30:23 is not correct.  You have to make sure that there is absolutely no diffuse glow from the emitting end of the laser source. Content: That light analogy doesn't hold up. With a laser, for example, you are not measuring the optimal path of many - you are measuring the one path which leaves point x and ends at y. A radiant light source, sends out an infinite number of paths of light from x with infinite destinations, all of which only travel over one path for each destination. Through a medium that deflects the light, it is an indirect path because the shortest approach will not reach the destination. In that case, the light doesn't decide where to go, the path and the destination decide the light's success.

Author: @dashcamacademy6457
Content: Not going to lie, this demo and explanation is bad science. Photons do not explore and set out to go to any point, they set out in a direction and travel by way of the path of least resistance and end up at their destination, a point WE label as point B. Where this Point B happens to be is not by way of the photon's exploration of many paths, but determined by the resistance it encounters. Simple defraction is what's going on in the demo: photons by defraction (i.e. "resistance") ending at Point B (i.e. camera). The reason multiple images are showing is that Point B shown in the demo isn't a single point but rather multiple points on the camera's image sensor (the sensor consists of a combined set of many points, making a single image). A photon can only take one single path to its one single destination given the particular resistance it encounters. IOW, change the resistance and its destination will change accordingly.

Content:
I really appreciate your breakdown of quantum mechanics and the idea that a particle can take multiple paths simultaneously from point A to B. From the quantum perspective, the probability amplitude for all possible paths definitely gives us a unique and fascinating way to think about reality.

That said, I’d like to offer a slightly different lens from the classical or physical science perspective: in our macroscopic world, the shortest distance between two points is still a straight line—unless the medium changes (like with light bending through glass or water). In that case, the environment influences the path, and what may look like “twisting the narrative” is really just accounting for those medium-dependent factors.

So while quantum mechanics speaks in terms of probabilities and multiple possible paths, I think it’s also fair to say that—once all variables are known—there’s a determinable path already defined by the environment. It’s not that either view is wrong, but rather that they are different ways of looking at the same phenomenon depending on the scale and framework.

Just wanted to share that angle—thanks again for the video, really made me think.

Author: @praveenbhokre6518
Content:
1. Feynman Path Integrals Are Mathematical Tools:
	Feynman’s idea is that particles take all possible paths, but only mathematically.
	In reality, we can’t observe or photograph photons taking every possible route.
	The interference from many possible paths determines the probability of where the photon is detected—but you don’t “see” these paths.

2. Laser Beams Aren’t Perfect:
	Real lasers scatter light from the edges of their aperture and lenses.
	That scattered light does not follow the main beam’s path, and some of it can be deflected or reflected even when the main path is blocked.
	If the mirror, wall, or any surface is shiny or diffusive—even partially—it will reflect scattered light toward the detector (camera).

3. What Actually Explains the Red Dot?
	It’s not the photon “taking a magical alternate route.”
	It’s most likely scattered light reflecting from the edge of the laser or nearby surfaces, reaching the mirror and then the camera.

👎 Why the Conclusion Is Deceptive

While the demo is cool, it’s an example of showmanship over substance. The presenter takes a known classical effect (scattered light + mirror reflection) and claims it’s quantum weirdness.

That’s like saying:
🧪 “A drop of water curved around a stone, so water must be exploring all paths!”

Fun metaphor, but not proof.

Author: @teejay818
Content:
I watched this video on a flight, and it blew my mind. For a moment, it felt like I’d glimpsed something deep—like light truly does take every path, and math can trace the shape of reality itself.

That night, while attending an event at a hotel, I stepped outside to get some air. A man jumped from the roof. He landed just feet from where I stood.

The world didn’t stop. Music kept playing upstairs. A curtain was eventually pulled across the windows. But the image stayed with me—and so did this video. I replayed it over and over in my mind. Something about it wasn’t sitting right. I needed it to be true. I needed something to hold onto.

Because sometimes, in the face of horror, people reach for science the way others reach for religion. Not for comfort, but for coherence. We need to believe that the universe has rules. That it can be understood. That light doesn’t just vanish into the void—that it traces every path, faithfully, even when we can’t see where it’s going.

Later, I read the critiques. Physicists and educators explaining how the experiment didn’t prove what it claimed to. That it was more metaphor than measurement. And I’ll be honest—it stung. Not because I demand perfection from science videos, but because in a moment of real-world horror, I turned to science for clarity. And what I got felt more like a show.

This isn’t an attack. It’s a plea. When we communicate science, especially to millions, we owe the audience more than just awe. We owe them truth—or at the very least, the humility to say when something is still uncertain.

Because some of us are watching while trying to process the unthinkable. And what we’re looking for isn’t special effects—it’s something we can trust.

Content: It's becoming obvious to more people-and you demonstrated it in this video-that a lot of these "experiments" and theories are simply made up, and have nothing to do with physical reality. For example, in the double split there is no proof that one single proton is being shot through the double slit, and that the light is taking "infinite paths". You obviously also can't have an "infinite amount of splits" in reality. You can fantasize about it in your mind, and you can create mathematics to represent what you've fantasized, but it's only in quantum theorists' fantasy minds that light "explores all paths". Feymamn's theory is absurd, because light will travel where it's pointed, and molecules will travel in the direction of a force applied - they don't have "SOME CHANCE to take any path." That is a fantasy; in real life they travel the path of classical physics. If you want to know the direction of light, simply turn it on. The bands of light will go through slits in the foil and bounce off the mirror, and won't bounce off areas of the mirror if it's covered. If you want to know the direction of a laser, point it in a certain direction. Your concluding sentence, "So light, and by extension everything really does explore every possible paths" is absurd, and has not been proven. "Most of the time the crazy paths cancel one another out" ... I'm really laughing as I type this - it's because the path that is actually observed is because the object obeyed the laws of physics - not because all other paths are canceled out. 😅 You can see quantum people get giddy, because they're a part of a special club where they understand the made up fantasy languageand mind experiments. Meanwhile, the rest of us are in reality simply turning on lights and observing where the light goes. You end with a "THEORETICAL physicist", which is exactly right; you are in a theoretical world that doesn't apply to material reality, until you include the laws of physics. Stop wasting your bright mind and do something that will actually affect material reality, and possibly even make people's lives better.

Content: Can we use this model concept? Electrons remain localized at source and detection points, while electromagnetic waves carry energy and information through space via field interactions. Key principles: Energy applied to source electrons generates electromagnetic waves propagating in all directions through the field. Wave behavior occurs in the electromagnetic field itself, not particle trajectories. Electrons serve as field interaction points rather than traveling particles, but when we measure (collapse function), we can only detect signals from electrons as particles. Electromagnetic waves create interference patterns in the field, producing observed quantum phenomena, as electrons can only be located at quantum positions. Screen electrons detect and localize wave energy, converting field excitations to measurable particle events.

Author: @davidj9977
Content:
This argument around the net "path phase" having meaning here is very suspicious, bordering on nonsense. Any paths that are changed in tiny amounts will have tiny phase changes regardless of whether they are efficient or elaborate, and thus if grouped will have a "long additive phase arrow". This does not explain why this model would favor "shortest" paths that are changed the least, vs crazy elaborate paths that are changed the least. 

There is also no explanation of why certain paths would be grouped into a collection vs other paths. Certainly of the infinity of crazy paths, an infinity of them will have *exactly* the same phase, and if grouped together, would have a longer "additive phase arrow" than short efficient paths with minor phase differences. Why aren't those paths preferred?

These problems would be avoided if the wavelength the phase exists on is so insanely long that in the infinity of paths there are no two paths with the same phase, in which case it's not phase at all.

Content:
I disagree with the basic premise.  Light doesn't follow one path.  It radiates in all directions.  You only see the light that reaches you.   

When you use a laser, it follows the path that you set it on.  In your diagram at the 2:00 minute mark, you lay out possible paths for light to take.  But those are not possible paths between A and B.  First, the laser is pointed in a specific direction, so there is only one path that originated from point A.  Second, the angle of refraction between two surfaces is a constant, so when light hits the interface, there is only one direction it can take.  

If your premise was true and that light takes the shortest path from A to B, then you could keep everything the same except move B to the left directly below A and the light would follow the path to find you.  But it doesn't.  It will still be hitting where B used to be.  

Technically, light takes the shortest path.  But it also takes the longest path.  Because it takes the only path.

Content: 18:00 - I don't think this is exactly correct (the comment about all paths including faster than light, etc). Only paths with the speed of light (in the media involved) are included. The path of shortest time is usually (mostly) unique, which is why that particular path doesn't encounter destructive interference. Whereas targets that are "off center" have a multitude of paths that arrive at the same time with a well distributed phase. If paths of variable speed were included, the straight path would encounter just as much destructive interference as any other path and therefore would not be preferred. Everything about interference as described in this video is built on the foundation of constant speed.

Content:
Sure! Here’s a simplified breakdown of the main ideas from Veritasium's video *"Something Strange Happens When You Trust Quantum Mechanics"*:

### 1. **Quantum Mechanics is Weird**

* At the tiniest scales (like particles), things don’t behave like we expect. Particles can act like both waves and particles at the same time.

### 2. **The Double-Slit Experiment**

* When particles (like electrons) are fired at a wall with two slits, they can create a wave-like pattern—like they went through both slits at once. But if we try to measure which slit they went through, they act like particles and don’t create the wave pattern. This shows that just observing changes what happens.

### 3. **Superposition**

* In quantum mechanics, things can be in multiple states at once. For example, an electron can be in two places at the same time until we look at it, then it "chooses" one spot.

### 4. **Entanglement**

* When two particles are **entangled**, what happens to one instantly affects the other, even if they’re far apart. This happens faster than the speed of light, which doesn’t make sense according to normal physics.

### 5. **The Observer Effect**

* The act of **observing** a quantum system can change its state. This means the universe doesn't have a set reality until we measure it—it's like reality is "created" by our observation.

### 6. **Why It’s So Weird**

* All these strange ideas are true, and they actually work. Technologies like **quantum computing** are based on these odd principles, and they’re making huge advances, even though they don’t make sense with our everyday experience.

### 7. **Trusting Quantum Mechanics**

* The video suggests that if we fully trust quantum mechanics, we have to accept a reality that's very different from what we experience in our everyday world. But it works—quantum mechanics is accurate, even if it’s mind-bending.

In short, quantum mechanics is strange and doesn’t match our everyday experience, but it’s proven to be true and useful in real-world technologies. The video explains how trusting quantum theory opens up a very weird but accurate view of the universe.

What you see here is simply some stray light going downwards onto the diffractive film. A proof would require to send photons out ONLY at an angle which would not hit the diffractive film in a straight line.

Not all possible directions:
While the idea of a particle "going in all possible directions" might arise from the superposition concept, it's a misunderstanding. The superposition is a description of the particle's state, not a description of its physical movement. It's important to remember that a measurement will collapse the superposition, and the particle will be observed to be in one specific state, moving in a specific direction.

Content:
I think there is some difference between the two slits (or infinite slits) experiment and the proof reflection experiment in the end using the laser and the foil. For the infinite slits experiment, the light source before the slits is a line source, from which the photons travel in all directions and thus reach all the slits. Whereas in the proof experiment, the photons from the laser can only propagate along the laser beam direction before reaching the mirror below. In other words, the path of the photons before reaching the mirror has already been determined and no photon will take the paths that lead to the foil at all. Content:
I love Veritasium. But this video is utterly misleading and misinterprets the effect when using the laser.
The diffraction off the grating and the restored visibility of the laser does *not at all* originate from the laser beam.
It originates from scattered light at the laser's front facet. 
If you looked at the laser from the point of the grating, you would see that scattered light. There is actually measurable light intensity
at the location of the grating. But that's far more intense than the expected intensity from the transverse profile of a Gaussian laser beam.
You simply *cannot* generate light from blocking out half of essentially zero illumination!

Another false claim is the argument that you must allow for different speeds at 18:25 in the video.
You have completely ignored the fact that defining the travel time requires making the frequency uncertain via a short light pulse length - or using well defined wavelength/frequency makes the pulse long and travel time ill-defined.
The interference of all paths is simply a result of purely local interactions in a medium that can carry waves. 
An excitation at any point in space will be the source of a spherical wave. That's what Huygen's elementary waves are.
Mathematically they are the Green's function for the differential wave equation. And those elementary waves propagate at the speed of light/sound or whatever wave.

Author: @chrispatriot
Content:
Takes all paths" is not an observation — it's a theoretical crutch. The idea that a quantum particle moves through every possible route isn't a discovery; it's a convenient abstraction, born out of our inability (or unwillingness) to track the actual path taken. It may serve as a useful mathematical model, but it reflects mathematical convenience, not necessarily ontological truth. In reality, the particle has potentiality — many options — but actualizes one path based on some real condition: field tension, quantum pressure, energy gradient, symmetry, or perhaps even consciousness. That’s not just a philosophical stance — it’s a call for empirical accountability. We need to stop hiding behind probability clouds and start asking: what chooses the path?

This lazy reliance on infinite parallelism skips the deeper natural principle we already observe in systems like electricity, water, fire — or lightning. Lightning could go many directions, but it chooses the one with the least resistance, the strongest connection, the greatest success. That’s determinism through attraction — not chaos. You're really looking at conditional actualization, not random possibility. This aligns more with Bohm's implicate order or pilot-wave theory, where the particle isn’t lost in infinite options but is guided by a deeper field — one that knows exactly where to go.

Author: @shepleonard8695
Content:
Because of this uncertainty in many equations you will see a particle represented by a probability cloud, or a wave, with the denser the part of the cloud or higher the wave the more likely it is for it to be in that location. That’s all very well and good, but QM takes this idea to the level of ridiculousness with quantum tunnelling.

A good summary of all the fudges that this is used to explain is on Wikipedia [4]. Let’s start with the most obvious use; a physical barrier. In the real world if an object, say a billiard ball, approaches a barrier, say the edge of the table, we know that it is going to bounce off the barrier, unless it is moving with such velocity is smashes through the barrier, breaking it in the first place. Not so with quantum tunnelling – if the uncertainty of the particle is so large that the width of the probability cloud/wave is larger than the width of the barrier, then when the particle gets so close to the barrier that the uncertainty suggests it might actually be on the other side of the barrier, QM says it CAN be on the other side of the barrier – in fact, if you shoot enough particles at the barrier some will inevitably magically appear on the other side of the barrier, without affecting the barrier in any way at all.

Similarly if a wave approaches the barrier, then some of the energy of the wave will magically pass through the barrier, proportional to the uncertainty. This is clearly rubbish – the uncertainty principle is just telling us we can’t know for certain where the particle is at a certain point in time, but if the particle is approaching a barrier from some distance we know that it will either bounce off the barrier or break it; the particle will not magically pass through the barrier as if it is not there. The same holds true for energy barriers – a particle either has enough energy to get through or it does not, whereas in QM if you throw enough low-energy particles at an energy barrier some of them will eventually get through.

Unfortunately QM hides this ridiculousness in many layers of mathematics, to prevent anyone from working out what is actually happening, unless they spend an inordinate amount of time looking into it.

Content: I watched this vid and gotta say, I see the double slit experiment differently. Content: 26:30 Laser light emitted by a laser diode is not narrowly directed but conical; part of it hits the collimating lens, while another part strikes the metal casing of the laser diode, where it is repeatedly reflected and scattered. Then the beam collected by the lens passes through the pointer’s output aperture, partially touching its edges and scattering again. At each stage, some light is scattered in different directions. That’s why, when looking at a laser pointer in low light, you can see light directly at the output — something that shouldn’t happen with an ideal laser source. However, in real lasers, secondary glow at the output aperture is always clearly visible. By placing a diffraction grating in the form of a film in front of a mirror, he created a diffraction scatterer for this side glow. The diffractor became its multiple secondary source — not with planar waves after it, but with spherical ones. And the mirror behind it reflects these waves just like all others — at the same angle at which the light hits it. And since the secondary source — the diffraction grating — is located a few millimeters from the reflective surface, and the wave after it is spherical, it reflects in all directions, including into the camera. But let’s emphasize it again: the camera is simply seeing stray laser beams scattered on the diffraction grating as a secondary source. Not some mythical probability distribution rays, but light scattered at the laser’s output aperture according to the laws of ordinary classical optics.

Author: @hippogriff
Content:
Imagine a particle—not as a tiny marble flying through space, but as a whisper of *possibility*. It doesn’t take one path from A to B. Instead, it explores *every possible way* it could go—all at once.

Some paths are straight. Some are curved. Some loop wildly. Each one sends out a tiny wave, like ripples in a pond. These ripples add together. Where they align, they build up. Where they clash, they cancel out.

What we see in the end—on a screen or in a detector—is not the path the particle chose, but what *survived* after all the possibilities interfered. The particle is not a traveller. It is the *result* of every route it could have taken, summed into one outcome.

So the universe doesn’t run on certainty or single paths. It runs on *overlapping possibilities*, and what we call reality is the pattern that remains after everything else cancels out.

Author: @daesikkim6368
Content:
As someone who majored in theoretical physics, I think criticisms of the demo that one should've used a sharper laser are missing the point of Feynman's argument.

Feynman's path integral formula for a single particle arises as an expression of the probability amplitude for the particle at a position x1 at some time t1 to be at a different position x2 at a later time t2, or stated differently, the overlap between the wavefunctions |x1,t1> and |x2,t2>. The wavefunction of a particle sitting at a certain position is a superposition of plane waves propagating in every direction, each with the same probability. These are the equivalent to the first segments of "all possible paths" in Feynman's picture. A proper setting simulating this initial state would be an isotropic light source that emits photons in all directions with equal probability.

Light from a laser, on the other hand, is amplified around a certain direction of propagation, and the components propagating away from this preferred direction are accordingly smaller. Using a laser with a narrower beam of light would only make it harder to observe the non-classical paths taken by the photons.

The goal of the demo isn't finding a spot of light where there was no light at all. An isotropic light source would illuminate every point on the mirror. But a camera (or a photodetector) fixed at a position over the mirror would see the image of this light source only at one spot on the mirror according to the law of reflection. Feynman's theory predicts that, by manipulating the surface of the mirror suitably (e.g. putting a diffraction grating film on it), one can make visible the light rays that are reflected at different spots and reach the camera. The first version of the demo using a lamp already did the job sufficiently well.

The fact that the demo can be explained by treating light as classical wave is not a loophole in the argument of the video. Feynman's path integral formalism is just one of several formulations of quantum mechanics and is mathematically equivalent to Schroedinger's wave picture. Whether you treat each photon as a wave-like object or a particle that takes "all possible paths" simultaneously, it has to be that you get the same predictions.

Content: The flaw with this experiment is in the need to accept that a laser is 100% collimated - and it isn’t. I can see the source of the laser in this experiment - in that I can see the red glow at the point the laser is emitting its light.  If I can see the light then some light is propagating towards the camera - and therefore we have to conclude that (a) light is propagating in all directions from the source (i.e. the laser is not 100% collimated - even if it is 99.99%, some light is spreading out in all directions) and (b) the diffraction grating will produce the effect seen.  This experiment doesn’t prove the many paths theory as it can be equally explained by normal wave theory.  Try putting a shield around the source to prevent non-collimated light from propagating towards the camera (and directly at the diffraction grating) and see what the result is - does the diffraction grating still produce the same effect?  Now THAT would be a cool experiment to show if the same result is obtained.

Content: I don’t really see how the experiment at the end proves the theory of light exploring every possible path. The “striped” paper used looks very refractive in itself. Also, we are able to see light not only from the spot of the laser on the table but also directly from the laser source. Which just means that some photons are not in the tiny beam of the laser source and do escape at angles. The photons escaping at angles are the refracted in the “striped” paper into the camera lens. I am not saying the whole theory is wrong, but I wouldn’t take this experiment as proof for it being right. Even a mirror will have a tiny bit of distortion, which are parts that reflect in a bit of an off angle. Now take that “striped” paper, it probably have an insane amount of off-angle reflections, which is also why it looks as it does to the camera. So it also will reflect the light-source at weird angles giving you that optical illusion of multiple light spots. It doesn’t prove that the photons following the straight path also checked all other paths first.

So cool! A technical point, the fact that light interferes from double slit does not mean the longer path had light traveling >c.

It would be extra cool if you were to use a pulsed laser and a timing detector to see if the light traveling the longer paths move at c, as expected, or greater than c.

Content: This is a great video to explain the ‘action’ theory - fantastic, also  Feynmann integral path approach which is accepted by most physicists.  But what if Feynmann is wrong - pure and simple? The model is useful but is it real?  If we start with Fermat and the ‘least time’ principle IMHO that actually doesn’t  really do anything that Snell’s law doesn’t give us anyway, going further ultimately the whole thing can be derived anyway from Maxwells equation.  Snells law arises from the encounter between the light wavefront and the medium - that is what is physically happening in terms of local oscillations in the media.  So yes, it’s a least time outcome but that’s an output of the optical pathlength summation through the medium dictated by the wavefronts interaction with the medium as it travels through it.  You can apply the same thinking to the curvature of light by gravity (GR) - the mass related distortion of space is essentially a new type of refractive index that bends the light into a curved path (because it’s a gravitational gradient index.). It’s important to recognise that Feynman was trying to reframe the entire wave theory of light in the light of the outcome of the photoelectric effect - he had to find a model to justify how a light particle ‘knows’ which way to go given that he had dropped a wave model which tells you why and how the light wave goes where it goes.   I’m not ruling out some of the spookiness of QM but I think that can be kept separate from the ‘light as stream of photons that explores every path’ model.  At the moment i think I don’t need Fermat and I don’t need Feynmann.  Light just does what it does, as a wave.  However we should always keep an open mind because it’s all still up for grabs.

Author: @martin1482
Content:
I'm really sorry. But that's nonsense! Especially the "experiment", which "proves that a photon takes all possible paths" ... (sigh). In this setup, there are so many chances for scattering at the light source (yes - even at the laser), the air (dust), and also the mirror! And then these "simultaneous paths" are only different photons which in fact took different paths.
I fear that the idea of how quantum theory works is still sort of obscure ... 
Maybe generally about this channel here. The mathematical things are really interesting and sound. But much of the physics contributions here seem only lurid. It's not that I would really comprehend the deep and profound riddles about quantum mechanics. But I'm really sure that there is way more than just the simple Feynman-Mirror explanation. I mean so how I understand Feyman, it is NOT REALLY MEANT that a quantum particle takes all paths ... simultaneously. Feynman's path-integral formulation (indeed fully compatible with Schrödinger's and Heisberg's formulations of QM) just reformulates the "shortest path" principle formulation by assuming all paths, and just "interfering" out all non-classical paths. That's just a mathematical way to express this optimization. And you can recognize that because the path-integral formulation is just a variational principle ... and optimization principle! If a photon would REALLY take ALL paths, conceivable ... how could you ever guarantee energy and momentum conservation. Specifically local conservation (which btw. are underlying the path-integral formulation thanks to Emmy Noether)?
Maybe one should really make a point about the difference of "reality" (whatever that might be ... is rather philosophical a question) and a "description of observations" ... Because between both is really a whole universe, which involve most of the debates about cognition theory (part of philosophy touched by Kant, Popper, Jaynes, Jeffreys,  Kahnemann, ... to name few of the really many). 
I find it ok to try to explain others the science also in simplified words ... But making it too superficial is imho fraud. I'm sorry.

Author: @jake.helzer
Content: Casper Møbius’ demonstration is interesting, but I think it’s being misinterpreted. The diffraction grating doesn’t reveal hidden quantum paths—it modifies the wavefront, changing how light is dispersed and creating an interference pattern. That’s why we see light at an ‘unexpected’ angle. This is a known optical effect, not necessarily proof of normally canceled-out paths becoming visible.

Author: @markfernee3842
Content:
I'm sorry. I know everyone loves the video and the production quality is very high, but you are guilty of conflating classical optics with quantum theory. Classical waves have real-valued amplitudes, whereas, the quantum wavefunction is complex-valued. This is a major distinction. Everything you've shown is easily explained using classical wave optics. Furthermore, the principle of least action, or for optics, Fermat's principle of least time is easily derived simply by requiring that a classical object has a unique path. This is how you derive the Euler-Lagrange equations. 

In quantum theory, one can adopt a wave-like picture, or a particle-like picture. The Feynman path integral approach is the particle-like picture, and this is why it is predominantly used in particle physics. However, both approaches are equally valid. Furthermore, the paths are not in real space, but rather an abstract configuration space. So the entire notion of a "path" is far more abstract. 

I think far more intuition about quantum mechanics can be gained by substituting the Planck and de Broglie relationships into the Fourier transform to give the quantum Fourier transform, from which the Schrödinger equation can be derived and the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship understood. This then takes classical Fourier optics to quantum mechanics and allows us some glimpse of the abstractions required. 

The bottom line is that quantum theory is rooted in the idea that interference phenomena are universal, which means Planck's constant is a fundamental constant of nature. This then means that we need to use complex numbers to describe reality (not real numbers). This is reflected in the fact that probabilities are calculated using the modulus squared of the wavefunction, which makes quantum expectation values distinctly different from classical expectation values. 

Unfortunately, all those who now think they understand quantum theory from this video have just been misled.

Author: @arnoldaltre_2706
Content:
Not related to this video, but hoping someone can look into this in details: Has Time Already Ended? A New Perspective on the Universe

What if time isn’t actually passing, but we’re just perceiving it that way? What if everything—past, present, and future—has already happened, and we’re just moving through it at a slow rate?  

This idea is supported by relativity, entropy, and the concept of a "block universe." Let’s break it down.  

---

### **1. Time Perception and Gravity**  
Einstein’s theory of relativity shows that **time slows down in strong gravitational fields**. The equation for time dilation near a massive object is:  

> **dτ = dt * sqrt(1 - 2GM / (rc²))**  

where:  
- **dτ** = time experienced by an observer  
- **dt** = time measured from a distant point  
- **G** = gravitational constant  
- **M** = mass of the object  
- **r** = distance from the mass  
- **c** = speed of light  

As mass increases over cosmic history, **time slows down relative to an external observer**. What if we’re just perceiving time at an artificially slow rate due to mass and entropy?  

---

### **2. The Block Universe: Everything Has Already Happened**  
According to the **block universe** theory, time is just another dimension, like space. The entire universe, from the Big Bang to the far future, already "exists" as a 4D structure.  

Spacetime follows the equation:  

> **ds² = -c²dt² + dx² + dy² + dz²**  

This means time is just a coordinate in spacetime. If an observer existed outside our universe, they would see **all events at once, as a completed structure**.  

---

### **3. Entropy: The True Driver of Time**  
The **second law of thermodynamics** states that entropy (disorder) always increases:  

> **dS/dt > 0**  

If entropy controls our experience of time, then we can define **subjective time (τ) as a function of entropy (S)**:  

> **dτ/dS = λ**  (where λ is a constant)  

Since entropy in the universe grows as:  

> **S(t) ≈ t³**  

we get:  

> **τ ≈ λt³**  

**This means our perception of time slows as the universe evolves.** In the early universe, time "felt" faster; today, it feels slow because entropy is much higher.  

---

### **4. The Big Bang Happened "Instantly" from an External View**  
If entropy defines time, then from an external perspective, **all of time happened instantly**.  

The rate at which we perceive time is approximately:  

> **dτ/dt ≈ t²**  

As **t → 0** (near the Big Bang), **dτ/dt → 0**, meaning that **from the outside, the entire history of the universe is already set**. We just experience it as a slow, unfolding sequence.  

---

### **5. Do We Still Have Free Will?**  
If time is already "mapped out," do we have free will? Yes!  

Think of a **maze**:  
- From above, the entire maze exists, including all possible paths.  
- Inside, you still make real choices about which direction to take.  

Even if the universe is fully structured, **we still navigate through it**, making decisions that feel real.  

---

### **Conclusion**  
✅ Time is **not fundamental**—it emerges from entropy.  
✅ We perceive time **slowing down** due to increasing entropy.  
✅ From an **external perspective, all of time has already happened**.  
✅ We still experience **real choices**, even in a fixed structure.

Content:
1. Light explores all possible paths before choosing the quickest path between two points. The path light chooses is the path you observe. 
2. The larger the particles, the larger the action. This leads to less variation in the number of paths which survive relative to the least action path. With such little variation, we get general relativity. The smaller the particle, the smaller the action until eventually, you are at a point where large variations create unpredictable and non-casual atmospheres. This is when we get quantum mechanics. 
3. My thoughts on how to begin to solve this issue - As energy increases (which is mass multiplied by the speed of light^2), uncertainty decreases since the number of possible paths which exist at that energy wavelength goes down. Therefore, if we are going to unite relativity and quantum mechanics, we are going to need to interrelate this principle with pathway collapse in a formalized and mathematical way. 
4. Entropy is defined as the proportion of energy that is available for useful work. As the amount of energy that can be used decreases, entropy rises. As the energy (and mass) of a system goes up, the amount of entropy increases. This is because the more ordered or defined the energy is, the less energy there is going to be available for useful work. Therefore, if we want to unite the fields, entropy would be a good unifying candidate. 
5. More energy and mass means more of an effect on space and time. Zero energy and mass means that space and time operate in a completely straight line. As the energy and mass of the system goes up, spacetime becomes curved and warped. Relativity assumes that spacetime curves while quantum physics assumes that spacetime is constant. It is my intuition that quantum mechanics is incorrect in automatically assuming that spacetime is fixed. Even in the quantum world, mind bogglingly small particles are going to have mass and energy which means that spacetime is going to be curved as a result. The curve is so mind bogglingly small however, that if we were to assume that it was 0, it would line up with our observations even though it was incorrect. We need to find a way to scale the effect of spacetime distortions regardless of weight or energy to unify the theories.

Content: The problem with quantum mechanics is, it explains uncertainty in measurement with a mythology of statistics. The role of statistics is very simple - in absence of the understanding of the truth of a system, you construct a model that approximates its behavior. By design, it's imperfect. Content: It's interesting to consider the role of the diffraction grating in this experiment. While some skeptics suggest that the grating might simply focus scattered light from the laser, creating the illusion of additional reflections, it's important to consider whether the grating is actually affecting the light's trajectory. If the grating is changing the light's path, we might expect the main laser beam to become slightly dimmer, as some photons are redirected along new, longer paths. However, if the grating is just focusing scattered light, it shouldn't impact the main beam's intensity. Experimental measurements of the main beam's brightness could help clarify whether the grating is truly altering the light's path or just focusing stray light.

Author: @edwardjenner1381
Content:
1. Math != reality.  It is a model of reality.  An electron is not a wave, it is not a particle.  It is an electron.  Waves and particles are models of an electron.  Quantum fields are models of their particles.
2. the waves we are summing (wavefunctions) may not even be physical - this is still a debate, especially as you need to include paths that are 'non-physical'.  We cannot observe or measure them directly.  They are simply used to compute probabilities.
3. the reflection/scattering experiments are not showing what you say (or infer) they are.  This is a deeper topic, but you can never physically see the wavefunction.  Your laser has a non-zero probability of light being seen at the scattering film, so is not perfectly uni-directional. 

Personally, I like this explanation and like the idea of 'all paths being taken' and everything being essentially an interference pattern of wavefunctions.  But this is fundamentally still a model.  A model we know is not complete.

Author: @redtoxic8701
Content:
I see many people criticizing the laser experiment and for valid reason - the tip of the laser is glowing from many different angles. BUT, despite the fact that this experiment would fail with a perfect laser, this still showcases the principle of stationary action. I will reiterate the video's explanation but with the extra detail needed to (hopefully) clear the confusion:

I will call the scattered light from the tip the 'leaked' light, and the 'straight' beam the 'main' light. Without the leaked light, the standard deviation of the beam profile of the laser is definitely too small to allow the main light to even reach the uncovered side of the mirror, regardless of whether the grating is there or not. This means that only the leaked light is relevant when considering the reflections from the uncovered side.

Now let's look at the probability that a leaked photon is recorded by the camera after bouncing off some point in a small region of the uncovered side, without the grating. Because of quantum mechanics, until measured, the photon is in a superposition of hitting all points of that region at the same time. However, because the action of the path "laser->some point in the small mirror region->camera" is not stationary, the phases of the different points of that superposition will be random once they reach the camera, and hence cancel out, as described in the video. This means the probability of the camera recording a leaked photon bouncing off any small region of the uncovered side of the mirror approaches 0.

What the grating does is block a subset of the the points of the uncovered mirror. If the blocked points are at the right distance from one another, for some of the small regions of the mirror the grating will let through exactly those points with constructive interference, and hence the camera will have a non-zero probability of recording a photon bouncing off such a region. When enough photons are fired simultaneously, that small probability will turn into a small intensity, which we can see in the video.

However, the fact that we can only see the leaked light means that the laser source doesn't add any more insight to the mechanism than the normal lamp does. If anything, it makes it harder to see because the intensity is much smaller.

Author: @harikrishnanpa8491
Content:
The first few minutes are a bit misleading. The swimmer decides which path to take to minimize the action. But in the light case, if you use a directional source like laser, the light doesn't decide the incident angle, rather, it is set by us. The refractive angle gets decided due to the boundary conditions on the interface. If you don't use a directional source, which is more appropriate for the comparison with a swimmer, then you will see the entire refracted beam and not just the shortest path one. What you said is not wrong though. The thing with lasers is that the directionality is a consequence of light traveling through extremely long distances (this is really an oversimplification, but for the sake of argument, assume that this is true) between exiting the resonant cavity. This already makes sure that the laser beam will take a direction which minimizes photon's action inside the cavity. More precisely, the distance traveled by a photon outside the cavity is so tiny compared to what it has already traveled inside, that most of the 'action', and therefore the direction of the beam, is decided based on what happens inside. Once this direction is decided, it cannot be changed too much. 

This brings me to the last experiment with the laser. I believe that it was flawed and you should not expect a random laser sport on the grating out of nowhere. Even if you see a spot, you should be able to explain why the grating decided to make that particular spot and not other equidistant spots (modulo some mapping on the grating plane). Recall that there were a bunch of spots in the non-laser light which can be explained by interference patterns.

Content:
As other commenters said, the theoretical part about path integrals is awesome, but the last demonstration is far from perfect.
Clean the beam (by passing through a couple of good dark apertures) so that you cannot see the output glowing, and you won't see it "reflected" from the "magic foil".

In the beginning Derek said that it's "local interactions" that govern the beam, and later he said that we don't observe "crazy paths" because they cancel out, meaning they correspond to nearly zero integrals. But it is exactly what creates the seeming locality. If the beam reflects from the mirror, and it is clean enough so that at all other points (except what we call the beam) it is pretty much zero, then it won't matter if one puts a blocking sheet or any "magic foil" around it - it won't produce nonzero from what already is zero. The path integral can be divided into parts/steps and if the first halfway gives zero, then no need to calculate the second half. BTW this is why in the later part of the video while drawing "all" possible paths, only straight ones were shown. Not a single curved one. Because in free space only straight ones survive.

There are absolutely many situations when path integral leads to unexpected results, but the last demo is not that. Those situations are well known diffraction and interference, double slit. If it is too normal for you, and you even find normal that all matter particles also can be waves - then I suggest to check the next step. Entanglement and second quantization, when we really see what does it mean for waves (that of course interfere all the time) to be particles. For those who interested in this I suggest checking the Hong–Ou–Mandel effect.

Author: @asdf7219
Content:
23:57 This is the foundation for Lagrangian/Hamiltonian Mechanics. Its a rigorous mathematical system that lets you actually calculate the path of least action.

The function inside the integral is the Lagrangian, and it can be arbitrarily defined (mostly).
This is like finding an minima by setting f’=0 and f’’>0. Except now the math is made to do this for functions - or “functionals”, which are functions, which take a function as an input and spits out a scalar value. Here, the integral is the functional, the scalar value is the action which you want to minimize. 

You can learn this by taking an Analytical Mechanics course. Prerequisites include: multivariable calculus, basic mechanics, and maybe some linear algebra.

The Lagrangian formulation takes coordinates and their first derivative (velocity).

The Hamiltonian formulas takes coordinates, and their “generalized momentum”. It’s useful because you can take (some) coordinate transforms that can make the resulting differential equations look really pretty and easy to solve.

This framework is the most modern way of understanding physics, and is used in statistical, quantum, etc… There’s also massive parallels in this to machine learning, to the Loss function.

Author: @bryant4488
Content:
I appreciate the attempt of a demo showing that light takes every possible path, however, as many others have mentioned this experiment falls short in some important ways. In any Gaussian beam there exists infinitely many higher order spatial frequencies (i.e. infinitely many angles that rays of light travel toward) following a Gaussian distribution as such seeing the diffraction pattern can be explained classically. A simple experiment that does show light takes every possible path is that of a single photon wave-packet interacting with a double slit. Since you have only one photon at a time any interference pattern you achieve can lead you to conclude that every photon "goes through both slits" (i.e. takes every possible path).
It would not be very difficult to setup this experiment (a viable detector would be costly) or contact a lab in the field to set it up for you.
Great video overall though.

Turn one on in a particulate free environment and you'll only see it when the stream hits an object and reflects or if it shines directly into your eye.  However, most lasers that I've seen have an objective lens which, as any lens will do, will diffuse or redirect some of that light allowing us to see the objective lit up by the light being directed through it.  What I'm getting at is that the prismatic foil that he laid down is picking up that light, vs the directed stream of light that is the product of the laser.  I don't think that he proved what he said he proved at that point.  I get that the photons of light fan out in an infinite number of directions, but the directed laser light by its very nature is directed in a single direction and is only visible when it reflects off of another object or particle and at that point, will reflect in all possible directions.  This is the principle behind laser guidance systems.  The only way that we can even see lasers as a beam of light is due to the air and other suspended particulates in the air, like dust or moisture. 

Please feel free to correct me if I'm wrong, this is how we learn after all.  Great work on these videos!

Author: @Imsarthakraval
Content:
My perspective is that observation, in principle, should not alter the outcome if the observer is ideal—meaning it does not interact with the system in any way. However, in reality, observation always requires some form of interaction, which consumes energy and affects the system.

Consider the classic double-slit experiment: if a single camera is placed to observe particles passing through the slits, it detects them without significantly altering their behavior. However, if a second observer (another camera) is introduced, some particles will interact with the new camera’s lens and then sensor, where their energy is absorbed(converted to electric signal to be exact) rather than reflected. As a result, fewer particles reach the primary observation point (which are absorbed).

Extending this idea further, if an infinite number of observers were introduced, each absorbing a fraction of the particles' energy, then theoretically, no particles would remain observable at the final detection point. This suggests that the mere act of measurement—unless perfectly non-intrusive—inevitably reduces what can be observed.

Author: @sooprcoomr4828
Content:
The demo is very inconclusive since I can see the laser leak from the source with my bare eye on camera. The laser is also a maximally classical source with well defined initial momentum, and momentum is also a variable in the Action since it is the Legendre conjugate to position. So the "possible" initial states are given by the inital momentum, and the states that go in the middle should classically be enveloped into the Gaussian optics profile. I mean, everything is a Gaussian. That's even an assumption to make when calculating using path integrals - Gaussian profiles. 

Everything discussed before Feynman is based on heisenberg or schrodinger mechanics, not the principle of least action. Schrodinger equation is based on a newton-second-law like idea for a probability spread, in my understanding. 

The path integral formulation only really is guaranteed to interfere fully into the classical trajectory if it is at a very strong action (S>>h). I am not sure I am convinced of the stationary phase assumptions applying everywhere. I am also not sure if this video explains why this has to be consistent with the Schrodinger ideas that we should have heard of (probability of cat), since cancelling phases does not necessarily allow for the S-matrix to me Unitary, i.e. probability to be conserved and the total probability of finding oneself somewhere in our universe to be 1. 

If we want to introduce this very complicated new concept, we should probably make it resolvable with concepts that are already prevalent in popular descriptions of quantum mechanics.

Author: @markdavis7397
Content:
This is misleading to the point of being almost wrong.  The reason the interference pattern appears in the camera is that the laser pointer is not perfect -  you can see scattered illumination from *any* angle at the tip of any laser pointer.   Some light is scattered in the direction of the diffraction grating, and - not surprisingly - hits the grating and generates an interference pattern. This pattern of course can be detected off to the side.    It's not that the light in the main beam has some "desire" to hit the camera sensor, and therefore - finding its direct path blocked - decides to take an alternate path.

The video is not exactly wrong, it is true that the wave function is technically non-zero at any distance.   But this is very theoretical.   The probabilities get ridiculously small even at tiny distances.  You could set up an experiment like this and wait the age of the universe and not see one photon do anything extremely bizarre.    You sure as heck are not going to get a visible artifact instantly on a camera sensor.  That artifact is definitely due to easily-visible scattered light from the tip hitting the diffraction grating.

Author: @jeffstevensenphotography3553
Content: I have some questions about this experiment set-up. First, the laser light spot on the mirror is very bright, so bright it can be seen with room lights on. (1) The diffracted spots we see with the lights off and the mirror covered are very dim, so dim the room lights must be off. You are using a digital camera, and is it set in automatic exposure mode? If so, when you uncover the mirror where the main spot of the laser appears, the spot is so hugely more intense than the diffracted spots that the camera adjusts its sensitivity to a much lower level to image the bright spot of the laser automatically; it likely does not have the dynamic range to still image the much, much dimmer diffracted spots. I presume the digital camera chip has its sensitivity reduced on the fly. This may be why the diffracted spots disappear; they are still "there" but the camera is incapable of recording them simultaneously with the main spot. (2) Is the laser a laser diode with a lens in front? In which case that lens will induce some diffuse scattering inevitably; with the lights off we see the light source as a blob as directly imaged by the camera recording the video, so we know some much lower intensity diffusing/scattering is occurring. Also, the diffraction grating is by definition diffracting the light, and I wonder if there is some interaction between the diffraction grating and that diffuse scattered light? This video may be recording not proof of least-path-goes-everywhere, but flaws in the experimental set up. I welcome answers that address my questions.

Author: @The2378AlpacaMan
Content:
The demo is really compelling (especially with the laser), but I think there are a couple potential objections

1) Adding in the shade and the foil changes the collective system (i.e. the system that includes the light, mirror, camera, etc), so you're not looking at the same physical system as you had without the shade and foil. This means you technically can't conclude the light in both systems is the same (i.e. you can't conclude light in the first system travels multiple possible paths even if light in the second system travels multiple possible paths)

2) You're not looking at one individual photon. You're shining many photons, and you're looking at the statistics of all those photons. It's still possible that each individual photon travels a definite path, but different photons travel different paths

Content: Agree with many others here regarding the laser demo.  Further to my previous post I also thought it looked fishy, so I bought some diffraction grating, it's dead cheap: you can get a largish piece for a fiver.  If you try to replicate this experiment at home, as I did, you won't see anything that can't be explained by light leakage from the housing at the tip of the laser (which you can also see in the video).  If you put some blocking card (as I did) around the laser so there is no direct path from the leaking light to the diffraction grating, you see nothing.  That's not to say the path integral / all possible paths explanation is wrong (I'm certainly not going to contradict Feynman, I'm sure it's right!), but this is an exceptionally poor demonstration because (a) it doesn't really demonstrate the claimed effect and therefore (b) just confuses everyone.  Must try harder.  Lab conditions, no light leakage etc.  Also you need to use a surface silvered mirror because a regular mirror confuses the result with multiple internal reflections.  Perhaps it can be make to work, but not as shown.

Author: @dozrFAB
Content:
I feel like a bigger deal is being made of the way light behaves than need be. A diagram of a light source and an end point is just a simplified model; it's not reality itself. Of course light takes every path; light radiates from its source in all directions. Therefore, of course the one we see is the path of least action; it is the midpoint of many overlapping paths that light took to arrive at its destination, so it will be the brightest/most easily observed. The entire principle of light detection relies on the relative differences between the luminosity of two objects/mediums. It's the same reason a person's eyes see blurred images; the lens is not focusing the light well enough and so you get many more of the paths of light hitting your retina and confusing your brain. By that logic, the world's most powerful lens would be able to only allow a single photon of light to be directed to a "retina" and all other light would be directed elsewhere. If such a ultimate lens allowed only a single photon's plank-length-sized path to be allowed through, it would behave like that diagram; and thus the only light that would enter it, by definition, is the path of least action; since the lens itself acts as a threshold of action which must be overcome to direct the light. Perhaps it is even the property of lenses that capture many different paths of light and, as they interact with the lens, the different sections of the lens normalize the action the light takes. 

Perhaps then there are lenses for more "solid" matter such as a basketball? What would serve as a lens to normalize the action of such matter?

Author: @Trading_Nerd
Content:
It's interesting to delve into when addition and multiplication can yield the same result. Here's a breakdown:

When dealing with pairs of numbers:
If you're looking for pairs of numbers (x, y) where x + y = x * y, there are a couple of key solutions:
(0, 0): 0 + 0 = 0 and 0 * 0 = 0
(2, 2): 2 + 2 = 4 and 2 * 2 = 4
However, if you're not limited to whole numbers (integers), there are infinitely many real number pairs that satisfy this condition.
When restricting to a single number:
If you are looking for a single number that when added to itself is equal to when it is multiplied by itself, then only the numbers 0 and 2 satisfy that condition.
Key takeaway:
The "2 + 2 = 2 * 2" situation is a special case.
It is important to remember that the rules of addition and multiplication are different, and this result is a unique occurance.

Content: Just 2 words: “faint” (with an ‘a’) and “dark”. Simple again: I don’t like using werds like “circle” and “cylinder” (for related reasons), but you CAN think of the grating as made of tiny long cylinders, making it a bumpy (albeit in a very precise pattern) mirror on a tiny scale. Again, the sideways glow is much fainter than the forwards LAZER BEAM. Which is exactly what you see in the reflections: faint reflection(s) from the grating (bumpy mirror made of long tiny cylinders), and the much brighter direct reflection of the forwards beam itself, which Casper is sending in the more obviously θi=θr direction. Author: @barefootalien
Content:
I'm not super thrilled with the phrase "really does" in this. I think it's easy to forget that, even as powerful as the principle of least action is, it's still just a model of whatever is actually happening in the universe.

Every path taken down the rabbit hole of Quantum Mechanics must necessarily end, at some point, in "We don't really know what's happening, but this is the best model we have to describe it." This is because we know, absolutely stone cold, that Quantum Mechanics is _incorrect._ It's the best we have. It's the most incredibly accurate description of some parts of reality we've yet devised, but it definitely doesn't describe all of it, and therefore it definitely isn't what's "really happening."

It's easy to forget, but in a video that made a big deal of the Ultraviolet Catastrophe and of Planck's mentor telling him that physics is "basically complete" I think it's really critical to remember that we are at _exactly_ the point Planck was, right now. We've solved the Ultraviolet Catastrophe, but we have others that are just as bad or arguably even worse.

Anyway, this is mostly pedantic. As a video to get non-experts excited about this, and get people thinking, this was very well done. A lot of the explanations and graphics are extremely similar to others on the topic, but the inclusion of the history was very nicely done.

The demo at the end, though... just... nnf. All that really showed is what diffraction gratings do. It doesn't need quantum mechanics to explain it at all, just classical wave mechanics. It was a physical equivalent of the _setup_ of a double-slit experiment, but without the punchline. Very cool, but I don't think it shows what you claimed it shows.

Content: Good example of a poorly executed experiment from 29:25 with the laser. That commercial laser pointer has a bright red light coming off every direction at the end of it, because of diffuse light caused by its lens. One can clearly see it around 29:50 in the video. So technically it does not differ from the small lamp used previously. One should put the pointer into a small tube to cover the exit point of the pointer and repeat this experiment. Also, it should be executed in a vacuum, to prevent false detection of light reflecting from air molecules, mist and small dust particles in the air. Also, even with maximum care, some diffuse light will remain because of the diffraction at the end of the covering tube. One should measure the intensity of that diffracted light and compare it to the detected light coming from the optical grid on the mirror. The conclusion can be accepted only if the reflected light is significantly higher than the remaining diffuse light.
