29:50 To quote a redditor:

"In the video, it is claimed that if you aim a laser beam to *not* hit a diffraction grating, a reflected laser beam can still be seen coming off the diffraction grating... "because the laser beam is taking all possible paths." This is simply an incorrect prediction. They do the experiment, and it appears to work the way they say. But it only works because the laser pointer has isotropic scattering coming off of the aperture (in other words, when a laser pointer is on, you can see a red glow on the tip of the laser pointer, and this glow is visible in the video). So the only reason a red dot is visible in the grating is that you're seeing the reflection of the isotropic light from the tip of the laser pointer. Nothing to do with the main beam. The result of the experiment is *just wrong.* And it helps bolster an overinterpretation of the physical realness of the path integral formulation of maxwell's equations. "

Author: @zk6912
Content:
There is a key point which is not discussed in depth in the video: the basic statement in Feynman path ingegral talk is that a particle or photon takes all **possible** trajectories in space-time and the interference of these trajectories will lead to the actual macroscopic path that the particle or photon will take. The emphase is on the word "possible". Here possible means that for example, if we block the light path the photons will not go through the block. Alternatively we can say that it goes through but the probability is extremely low. For example, when Fayman explained how a mirror image of a light source is formed, he took natural, that the photons do not go through the mirror, rather they get reflected. Hence he considered the mirror as a constraint that limits the possible path of the photons. He excluded the half space and did not take into account the photons which goes through the mirror. However, for a complete explanation he should have taken it account, but he ignored, because he knew from every day experience, that their contribution is negligible. How can we generalize this observation? We can say that there are light modes which satisfy the boundary conditions. The photons which leave the source can propagate only in the possible light modes. In case of the laser the light modes are determined by the laser resonator: they are results of intereference effects which occur in the laser resonator. The light modes are such that the maximal probability of finding a photon is along the optical axis determined by the laser resonator. As we move away from the optical axis the probability of finding a photon gets smaller exponentially. This is why the laser light forms a beam. The light modes can be viewed as a contraint which determines the photon path outside the laser resonator.

In case of an LED or ordinary light bulb, there are no optical resonators. Hence the photon modes are spherical waves which may propagate in all possible direction. There is also some blocking, for example in cas of an LED the back plate of the LED is a block (or constraint), and for the light bulb the mount of the bulb is a block for light as well. Hence Feynman explanation is valid for the LED or light bulb. For the laser light it is also true, but the properties of the light source should be taken into account: when the photons leave the laser resonator, there is high probabilty that the photons move along the optical axis of the laser resonator, and as we get farther from the optical axis the probabilty gets exponentially low.

Content: There is a hidden assumption in the concept of “exploring all possible paths” and that is “there are paths”. Instead of “exploring all possible paths” it could be “considering all possible moves”, as in chess.  Interactions are discrete and there is nothing (no path, no wave, no particle) between interactions, there is only the Diophantine mathematics defining the relationships between interactions.  This viewpoint makes the weirdness of quantum experiments, as well as Zeno’s paradoxes, make common sense.  The goal then becomes, not finding the final Lagrangian, but finding the final Diophantine equation.

Content: This interpretation goes far but not far enough to fully explain quantum physics. You can prevent a quantum particle from taking multiple paths by making available information about which path it took. This causes the superposition of all possible paths to collapse and the particle behaves classically, taking only a single path seemingly without doing any exploration of other paths. This is shown experimentally in the double slit experiment by putting a detector at the slits. This makes the particle unable to interfere with it's other possible paths between the slits and the screen and a classical distribution is observed on the screen, rather than an interference pattern of it interacting with its other possible paths.

There are two tricky points:

If there is an infinite number of slits, this effectively means there are no distinct slits at all. However, still we see the interference pattern?

2. Regarding the last experiment: Even if the laser initially produces a flat wavefront, placing foil onto the mirror surface effectively creates a diffraction grating. According to the Huygens–Fresnel principle, when the wave reflects from this diffraction grating, the reflected wavefront is no longer flat, but rather consists of spherical waves propagating in all directions. As a result, the reflected waves become visible in the camera.

Content:
The Nature of Reality: Action, Entanglement, and Wavelengths

Most people think of reality as a series of events that happen in a straight line—past leads to present, which leads to future. But in reality, past and future are not separate—they are a single entangled field.

Everything we see as motion, time, and even choice is actually the result of oscillations within this field. The present moment is not a fixed point—it is a wave function that exists in superposition, meaning it is always shifting between different possibilities before stabilizing into something we observe.

Why Everything Has a Wavelength

The reason everything has a wavelength is because particles are not fixed objects—they exist as both waves and particles at the same time. This means that what we think of as “movement” is not a straight path, but a wave oscillation between different possible states.

Light doesn’t just travel in a straight line—it explores all possible paths at once.

The reason we only see one path is because all the other possibilities cancel out through interference.

This same principle applies to everything that exists—from atoms to planets to thoughts—everything is governed by wave-like behavior.


The Role of Action: The Hidden Organizer of Reality

In physics, there’s a quantity called action, which describes how a system moves from one state to another. Everything in nature follows the path of least action—the most stable, lowest-energy way for something to exist.

This is why:

Light bends when passing through different materials—it is taking the fastest path.

Electrons in atoms don’t spiral into the nucleus—they exist in stable orbits that form standing waves.

Planets orbit stars in predictable paths—their motion is not a straight line but a continuous balancing of forces.


Action is what determines which possibilities become real and which cancel out. It decides which wave patterns constructively interfere (reinforce each other) or destructively interfere (cancel out).

Past, Future, and the Present as a Standing Wave

Instead of thinking about time as moving forward, imagine it as a standing wave, where the past and future are simply different points on the same structure. The present moment is like a node on this wave—a place where interference patterns stabilize just long enough for us to perceive them before shifting again.

This means:

Time isn’t flowing—it’s resonating.

The universe isn’t moving forward—it’s balancing itself between entangled states.

Reality isn’t “changing”—it’s constantly resolving interference between possible outcomes.


What This Means for Everything

When people talk about the search for a “Theory of Everything” in physics, what they are really looking for is the equation that describes this wave-field of reality—the mathematical formula that explains how everything stabilizes within this oscillating system.

But the truth is, this process is already happening everywhere:

Every decision we make is not a “choice” in the way we think—it is a resolution of interference patterns within our own wave function.

Every motion in the universe is not a straight line—it is a balancing act of entangled possibilities collapsing into the most stable configuration.

Everything we experience is not separate moments in time—it is a continuous resonance of waves interacting across the field of existence.


Conclusion

The universe isn’t made of separate objects moving through time—it is an entangled field of waves and particles, past and future, all oscillating in a synchronized, self-stabilizing system.

What we perceive as “motion” or “time” is actually the resolution of interference patterns within this system.

So in the deepest sense:

Reality isn’t progressing—it’s resonating.

Time isn’t moving—it’s balancing.

Action isn’t force—it’s the organizing principle that keeps everything in harmony.


Everything we do, everything we see, everything that happens—it's all just wave interference settling into the most stable possible state.

Content: I am a bit disappointed from this video, although usually I am a great fan and i have already learned a lot from this channel. But the experimental demonstration that Casper did and explained, is misleading in my opinion. The foil with lines on it, is exactly the same as what a grating does. If i remember correctly, Feynman also said this in his outreach book on QED. The foil facilitates the reflection also at this angle. In case of the laser, the foil allows that the image of the laser from the side can be reflected at this angle as well into the camera. If you look at the laser from the side, you also see a little bit of a red light from the side that is leaking out of the aperture. That does not mean that the laser beam tries all possible ways to find the camera or that it deviates part of its power into the camera, as the video insinuated. The part that ends up on your camera is not part of the actual laser beam, but it is light, that has been leaking in a diffuse way out of the aperture or beam. That is just classical imaging and reflection from the grating, it has nothing to do with the laser itself. I think it is a very misleading way of teaching the principle of least action. I agree with the explanation for the case of diffuse light, though.

Author: @Watykaniak
Content: I must correct a common misconception here. The path integral formulation doesn't claim that particles literally take all possible paths in the classical sense, nor does it suggest that we should expect these absurd paths - like a particle reversing or taking wildly improbable routes - to be observed in reality. Instead, what Feynman’s framework suggests is that all paths are mathematically possible, but they contribute to the overall probability based on how likely they are. The paths that are closest to the classical trajectory dominate the result, and the strange, unlikely paths contribute only marginally. To say that particles "follow" all these paths is misleading and misrepresents the statistical nature of quantum mechanics. It's about probability, not physical motion. This theory isn't about particles behaving in a whimsical, impossible way - it's a tool for calculating the likelihood of different outcomes. Let's not confuse the theory's mathematical tools with physical reality

Author: @DiegoCasadei
Content: Thanks again for your beautiful work!  Let me here focus on the last part, the "demonstration" that photons explore all possible paths.  Your experiment does not actually prove it 🙂 even though it's fantastic.  This is how I would address it.  You might want to consider this for a future video.  First, the laser beam shall go through a black pipe that ensures no scattering at the laser output sends photons to the grating. A telescopic pipe (i.e. two nested ones) would help you testing that at some point the "source" of reflected photons on the grating is outside the geometrical field of view of the laser.  If you still see light spots on the grating, the next step is to eliminate (or reduce) the diffraction from air.  For that, you need to work inside a vacuum bell.  By decreasing pressure the amount of scattered light decreases, dimming the light spots on the grating.  If the decrease is not proportional to the air density, then there is a hint that photons may explore non-rectilinear paths.  Feynmann integrals, as far as I (mis-)understand them, are not setting constraints on the trajectory.  Therefore, curved paths are in principle possible.  I could be wrong of course :-) All the best! Author: @peoplez129
Content: The whole problem with this is people completely misunderstand the double slit experiment. When you change "observation" to "interaction", the actual reality becomes clear. Basically the double slit experiment is misinterpreted. What they do is use photon detectors, which actually interact with the photons as they pass through the slit. When you turn the detector off, no interaction occurs, therefore light does what it would naturally do. So it's not an issue of observation, but they are changing the result through direct interaction. This is why the double slit experiment isn't what people think it is. The double slit experiment is actually a big nothingburger that has been overhyped because of the way they chose to describe it, which makes it sound like more is going on that what actually is. But it's nothing more than like putting a flame under a pot of water and then saying "voila, the temperature has changed by magic just by me looking at it!". It's not magic, you just interacted with it, and as the saying goes, every action has an equal or opposite reaction. Or in other words, no there's nothing particularly special going on.

Author: @koka3243
Content: Hey! Thanks for another video on QM! Just a comment from a guy whose PhD thesis title happens to contain both words, quantum & mechanics: the experiment with the laser is actually no more convincing than the one with a point light source since the "faint red dot" you're seeing in the reflection from the diffraction grating with the laser as the source is essentially the diffracted image of the red glow of the laser's opening as you see it with your own eyes: indeed, you can see the laser is "on" without needing to look straight into the path of the light — that red dot that you see at the point where beam exits the body of the laser (visible around 29:50) is just some stray photons that come out due to all sorts of imperfections in the laser's optics/silicon. Now, you can actually try to suppress that stray light by cutting a hole in a sheet of black paper just large enough for the entire beam to pass through and making the laser beam go though that hole as it begins its journey. You won't see the red dot of the laser opening anymore, and you won't get the "faint red dot" with the diffraction grating either. Try it for yourself!  In fact, you don't even need a laser for this — make a light from a bulb pass though a hole in a black sheet of paper (this process, actually, has a name: collimation) and you'll have the "faint red dot" disappear as well. The end result: for the diffraction grating to reflect any light the photons have to have non-vanishing probabilities/amplitudes to come to the diffraction grating in the first place. Amazingly, you can actually create light (and even single photons!) that only travel along a straight narrow path. Collimated light is precisely the type of light for which the probabilities/amplitudes of photons reaching any point outside the beam of light are vanishingly small. Hopefully, this will make sense. Now, a couple of words for physics students: for a photon that comes from infinity (i.e., plane wave) and goes through any hole in an otherwise opaque flat screen that's perpendicular to the direction of the photon's wave vector, its amplitude on the other side of the screen is obtainable in a nice closed form (formula) for any point of the half-space, but is especially simple at infinity where it becomes a 2D Fourier transform of the so-called support function of the hole, i.e. a function that's defined for points on the 2d screen and is 1 inside the whole and 0 outside. And so, a) for very small holes (support function is Dirac's delta) the Fourier Transform is a constant — small holes become secondary point sources of light that radiate equally in all directions; b) extended holes (of sizes many times the wavelength of light) have the radial diagram that has a high peak for angle = 0 to the normal of the plane (i.e. the direction of the original photon), with a very strong fall-off (the angular width estimate is the well-known "lambda-over-D"); in particular, the resulting angular distribution for a circular hole was calculated for the first time by Fresnel and bears his name (the Fresnel integral). So, the recipe for having a perfectly collimated light beam has two ingredients: take the light source to infinity and make the hole as big as possible. You go an extra step by making your hole have its transmission coefficient transition more smoothly from 0 outside the hole to 1 inside — make it a (2D) Gaussian function and you've got yourself the so-called Gaussian beam on the other side (google it for its wonderful properties). P.S. The moral of the story: collimate your beams, or otherwise you might end up discovering "quantum effects" that have nothing to do with the quantum properties of light ;-)

Author: @mr.username
Content: Great video, but the final laser demonstration is unfortunately misleading. Roughly speaking, with the path integral formulation you have to additionally integrate the amplitude over the area of the laser aperture where we consider our light source to be, as the fixed-point initial condition does not apply anymore. This will effectively create the same destructive interference that makes the laser beam an exponentially-well-confined beam (a Gaussian beam). So what we see on the camera is a simple light spill from some reflections.

Two things.
One: I don't see how so many people say they are surprised by this given that I learned this in second year undergraduate physics in 1986.  Has education fallen so far?

I was taught to think of light as a wave, and a particle as an event (not an object). Author: @DaveEtchells
Content:
Good video, but *_The final demo was ridiculous and incorrect_*
It has nothing to do with light taking all possible paths, it was nothing more than the off-axis light from the tip of the pointer (which you can clearly see from the viewpoint of the camera filming the experiment) being diffracted back into the lens of the experiment’s camera. The implication in the video was that the light from the main beam of the laser was somehow bending back in space to diffract off of the grating, and that's not remotely the case. The off-axis light is just side-lobe radiation from the laser beam, or reflection off the laser housing or optics, striking the diffraction grating following a straight path.

The rest of the video was excellent, but for heaven’s sake *_think_* about what’s being shown in demos vs getting so caught up in the story that you lose sight of what’s actually going on.

Author: @JamesJaber-x5p
Content:
Hi @veritasium,

This was an absolutely fascinating and mind-expanding video! It not only clarified many concepts but also started to shed light on why things behave the way they do. That said, I was hoping the video might touch on a question that has always puzzled me about the double-slit experiment—specifically when firing single particles (such as electrons) one at a time, the interference pattern still emerges!

My thought experiment is as follows: If we fire a single electron every hour (or even once a day!) for 10,000 years, how does the familiar multi-bar interference pattern still form? How does each subsequent electron "know" where to land on the screen so that, over time, the overall interference pattern emerges?

The video beautifully explains the probabilistic nature of a single particle’s path—how it follows a distribution with peaks at constructive interference points, troughs at destructive interference points, and a spectrum of intensities in between. However, what I’m still trying to understand is how this seemingly independent behaviour of individual particles collectively results in such a well-defined interference pattern over time.

One hypothesis I’ve been toying with is whether the behaviour of each electron might be linked to the others at the moment of their creation. Could it be that each particle has a predetermined collapse point even before it is emitted? A wild thought, perhaps—but as this video highlights, many aspects of quantum mechanics seem counterintuitive to our macroscopic perspective!

Would love to hear your thoughts!

Author: @axle.student
Content:
Thanks. I found this very helpful.
I am not a physicist, but I actually "Get it" from a number of different perspectives. This kind of bound all that together for me in a descriptive sense.
>
This is where my predominant perspective differs from mainstream. I see everything as fundamentally non-discrete. The discrete part kind of emerges out of it, or we kind of force it to emerge for the sake of our discrete math.
So in that context there is not infinite paths but a single very wide path. You could imagine this as the circumference of a circle representing a single path from the center, except only one infinitesimally small section (amplitude) of the standing wave is visible in the classic world.
Action is central, it is the fundamental component of the universe. I often use motion or flux to represent a universe that is non-static. Everything is in motion and never stands still as a discrete point. It is always in a constant state of flux.
I often bang on about circles (and spheres) as the primary representation of the universe and use the word "Analog" a lot. Circles are never discrete and never stand still; they are in a constant state of flux. (Imagine spinning a perfect circle. It still just looks like a static circle.)
Yes we see what appears to be discrete or static at the apex of the standing wave, but it is a fuzzy point always. Uncertainty principle highlights this "fuzzyness" in the curve at the apex of amplitude in the wave. The entire circumference of a circle is a fuzzy amplitude.
.
I am not painting the full depth of the picture above. Once you see the universe as a continuum in a constant state of flux, many things begin to make a lot of sense. Even entanglement makes perfect sense without any spookyness :)
.
P.S. You can use time, but I find it better to completely remove time from your thinking. In some sense this forces everything in the universe to always be correlated across that moment and it is only the phase of the action (Position of the wave or circle) that changes rather than time.

Content:
Planck’s discovery of the correct constant reminds me of the small-world network theory.

Content: This is still just a fun little accounting trick that comes to the same conclusions as the classical ones, but in a potentially easier way. Consider that when taking the modulus of an extremely large number divided by a smaller number, which is what you talked about here, it doesn't matter whether we're talking about 1,001 vs 1,002 or 1,000,001 vs 1,000,002, they'll both have the same modular distance. So if two paths don't cancel out when they're similar, it doesn't matter if those two paths are similar to the actual one or very different from the actual path, as long as they're similar to each other. So looking at your models in the video, if I take one of the very long, winding paths, modify it very slightly a few times, and then put the resultant paths through the same filter, I'll end up with a very high probability of a wave following one of those paths. Even though the paths are obviously wrong.

Author: @tnb178
Content: The claim that a particle physically takes all paths is a misconception. The Schrödinger equation is equivalent to the path integral, which is merely a reformulation of the former, not an independent principle. Quantum evolution is fully described by local wave dynamics, as all experiments confirm. Your video itself derives the path integral from the wave equation, proving their equivalence. The existence of global and local descriptions says nothing about reality. Only probabilities are observable. The true nature of the particle’s motion is a matter of interpretation of the different mathematical descriptions. This is the domain of philosophy, not physics.

Author: @johannpascher
Content:
Comment by Johann Pascher  

The video offers an engaging visual exploration of quantum concepts, particularly in its treatment of light behavior and the idea that particles explore "all possible paths." However, several clarifications are essential to untangle the mathematical framework from the physical interpretation. Here’s a refined perspective that aligns with the themes raised:  

The visibility of a laser beam hinges entirely on its interaction with matter. In a vacuum or perfectly clear air, a laser remains invisible because light—whether classical or quantum—requires scattering off particles like dust or aerosols to become detectable. This isn’t a uniquely quantum phenomenon but a classical principle: light travels as an electromagnetic (EM) field, and detection depends on photons interacting with a measuring device, whether a camera sensor or the human eye. From a quantum viewpoint, photons exist as delocalized probabilities until measured, but the act of measurement itself is a contentious topic. Interpretations vary, but the core takeaway is that observation localizes what was previously a spread-out probability amplitude.  

The video risks conflating the electromagnetic field with classical wave imagery. The EM field is not a literal wave in the sense of water ripples but a fundamental entity that permeates all space. A laser approximates a tightly focused plane wave within this field, yet even its "collimated" beam diverges slightly due to diffraction. What we perceive as a confined beam is a practical consequence of coherence and directional alignment, not a violation of the field’s infinite reach. The energy density drops exponentially outside the beam’s core, rendering the field’s effects negligible in everyday observation, but mathematically, it persists everywhere.  

Classically, a laser is modeled as an electromagnetic wave solution to Maxwell’s equations. Quantum mechanically, it’s described as a coherent state of photons—a collective quantum behavior where individual photons lack defined paths but statistically mimic classical waves. This duality underscores a key quantum principle: what we observe macroscopically (e.g., a focused beam) emerges from the probabilistic behavior of countless particles. Each photon’s detection is a localized event, but their aggregate behavior reconstructs the classical wave pattern.  

Your emphasis on the EM field’s spatial extent is valid but requires nuance. While the field exists everywhere, its observable influence is concentrated in regions of high energy density, such as the laser beam. Outside this zone, vacuum fluctuations—a quantum feature of empty space—dominate, though these are unrelated to the laser’s field. The beam’s apparent confinement is thus a matter of scale and practicality, not a contradiction of quantum non-locality.  

Central to this discussion is quantum mechanics’ role as a probabilistic theory. Feynman’s path integral method, while elegant, calculates probabilities by summing amplitudes over all conceivable paths. These paths are mathematical constructs, not physical trajectories. Just as a navigation app computes optimal routes without implying a driver traverses all possibilities simultaneously, the path integral quantifies likelihoods, not literal histories. Experiments validate statistical outcomes, not the "reality" of paths.  

The video’s strength lies in demonstrating non-classical phenomena, such as interference from counterintuitive paths. However, it blurs the line between calculation and ontology. To enhance clarity, the narrative should stress that quantum mechanics predicts probabilities, not certainties, and that measurement transforms quantum possibilities into classical facts. The electromagnetic field’s existence isn’t contingent on observation, but its detectable effects are.  

By foregrounding these distinctions, the video could avoid conflating mathematical abstraction with physical truth—a subtlety vital for grasping quantum theory’s profound yet often misunderstood implications.  

Johann Pascher

Content:
This is a fascinating, and to me and others mind BENDING video Derek.

But you have many folks in the comments identifying as physicists who are pointing out that there are significant problems with this demo, and its not showing what is purported to be showing.

Can you and your guests perhaps elaborate on this and tighten up in an actual experiment to rule out their concerns?  

For example copying from sub-comments:

"I don’t understand what was special about the demo. There are bazillions of photons coming out of that laser. Some small portion of those photons don’t come out straight with the main laser beam. They come out as off-center photons and interfere with themselves cancelling their chance of reflection unless someone puts a filter in that area that removes the interference, which allows those off-center photons to reflect. So there is nothing surprising here in my view.

Now in regards to what I’m calling off-center photons, if one could prove that these photons being exposed by the filter actually reduces the number of photons being reflected in the main beam (preferably shown by sending one photon at a time), then that would be convincing that a single photon is taking all paths. But the demo in this video didn’t do that and isn’t really convincing of anything."

and:

"The laser experiment does not show what it purports to. If you look at 29:42, I can clearly see the laser is turned on at its tip, even though its pointing about 90 degrees away from the camera. So what is being demonstrated is the poor beam quality of this laser. If it was a pure gaussian beam with no scattering at the aperture of the laser, the path integral would already destructively interfere before getting to the grating, and having a grating or not having a grating would not make a noticeable difference, even if you should technically include those paths in the integral, and the contribution would not be absolute zero. Content:
I think the core part of the explanation, which you've kind of skipped, is how the quickest path manifests in that interference pattern as the only visible trajectory. In other words, how come the fastest path is suddenly not randomly distributed and not destructively interfering with its close neighbors?

If I understand it correctly, it is less random in that neighborhood, because the optimality corresponds with a lot of paths having similar action quantities. And since the action graph has a minimum around that point (derivative close to 0), the graph is flater there - a wider family of similar paths corresponds to a very similar range of action. And so there are many, many more paths close to the optimal one with almost same action and phase, so they interfere constructively, enough to overcome the randomness.

Author: @sirgatomcgatinson5711
Content:
The video is super nice, congrats.
However, I think there's a problem with the interpretation of the experiment in the end, and that it's not really proving a quantum effect. It's just a classical diffraction experiment.

The main point of the video, the exploration of all possible paths by the particles in their movement (path integral formalism), is not actually a "physical point to be proven", but rather an alternative framework to "wave-function stuff" for calculations in quantum mechanics.

The whole point of it is that using either wave-functions and co. or using the path integral formalism provides the same results in physical calculations. So the path-integral formalism is just a different way of doing "same old quantum mechanics".

If we then get to the experiment at the last part of the video, that's simply a standard diffraction experiment with light. Classical electromagnetism is already enough to explain it, without the need for quantum mechanics.
The "pseudo path integral" explanation in this case is only working as a reinterpretation of electromagnetic wave mechanics, in an analogous way as normal path integral does with wave-function mechanics in QM.

There's a problem with the demo: The laser diode isn't collimated. You can see stray light from "all" angles of the diode. It can be seen by the camera almost perpendicular to the diode, to illustrate the point.

Measure the brightness and it changes.

If the light could take any path then when the lowest action path is covered, the brightness in the new lowest action spot would be the same. But in this experiment it decreases, because different light is taking a different path that it was always taking.

Author: @nikbl4k
Content:
The Exception: Paths Near the Least Action Path

There’s one special case to the paths all canceling out/interfering: paths for which small variations don’t change the action much. These paths have very similar actions, so their phases stay coherent (aligned), leading to constructive interference.

The stationary phase principle says that constructive interference happens where  is stationary (i.e., where small changes in the path don’t change  much).

These are the paths closest to the classical path—the one satisfying the least action principle.

This explains why, in the classical limit, the quantum path integral overwhelmingly favors the classical path.

The part I'm having trouble wrapping my head around is that when you say particles travel from A to B..... why? Electrons don't have a destination, they're just moving. Author: @medteqsupportvideos2863
Content: This video hits at the fundamental flaw in quantum mechanics, the assumption that in order for a particle to create an interference pattern, it must pass through both slits as a wave, and thereby interfere with *itself*. It discounts the possibility that all the particle is doing is disturbing spacetime and it is this disturbance that travels through both slits. It's also possible that spacetime itself is random and the particle is deterministic, and also the possibility exists that a presence of a particle might influence (e.g. reduce) local randomness, and it is this effect that travels through both slits. The math for these options would be horrendous, but they are much better solutions conceptually than particle wave duality, multiple worlds, action at a distance all the weirdness arising out of the "Copenhagen interpretation". The assumption that light travels all possible paths then appears simply as a math trick, but not a true representation of reality.

Content:
Your producer said at one point "these two paths are different lengths. So clearly, they didn't have the same speed". That does not make sense. 

A wavefront F can interfere constructively with with another wavefront of F + n*λ where λ is the wavelength and n is any integer. They don't have to travel at different speeds through slits to interfere at different points on the wall.

Also "stationary action" is maybe more correct than "least action". What's wanted is not a strict minimum, but a max or a min. The action won't change to first order at a max or a min.

Author: @jeremycull8876
Content:
Good video - there is a problem I'd like to point out. The uncomfortable intuition associated with "all possible paths" and "multi-verse" is that it restricts what is fundamentally more wave-like to something we can grasp in everyday life. The wave-particle duality isn't the whole story about what it is, there are subtle characteristics associated with how we characterize "particle" and characterize "wave". An over-simplified but useful way to think about it is that a particle is that feature of a wave that is somehow being made present that we can measure. Measured in such a way that the wave properties themselves need not be measured. Depending on the "particle behavior" we care about. De broglie's concept of standing wave and the net interference that results explains so much. We use the probability concept to model the wave properties, but really the wave properties are the more fundamental concept, not the probability... At least this is what I believe. You can't explain the collapse of the wave function by probability, but you may be able to explain the collapse by the properties of waves.

It's a weird thing to say that something "physical" is more fundamental than something like probability... But I think this is true. They often like to tie geometric phenomenon to probability, as if probability gives rise to physical reality itself. But why can't the opposite be true? Probability is a convenient feature of the predictability associated with physical phenomena and its laws. It's useful and interesting, but hardly explanatory.

Next video idea: compare and contrast waves and probability.

Author: @reinoguri4405
Content:
In this experiment it is assumed that by seeing 2 dots from the same light source we prouve that that light took 2 different paths to go from point A to point B, but in reality one dot represents light going from point A to point B and the other light going from point A to point C (another pixel since the 2 dots), so one photon cannot light 2 pixels at the same time since it can only transfer one packet of energy to only one of the pixels, so in this experiment we just observed 2 different photons following 2 different paths and hitting 2 different pixels in the end. At no point can we correlate this to one photon exploring 2 different paths to go from A to B. I am not going against the theory I am just saying this experiment doesn't prove it at all.
I think this theory cannot be proven with a camera sensor at all. The way the camera sensor processes information into pixels assumes that light travels in a straight path. However, in this case, our theory suggests that light takes alternative pathways, making turns as it explores. Yet, our sensor (and our eyes, which work similarly) can only interpret straight paths—or, more precisely, the path of least action.

It is impossible to determine the exact trajectory the photon followed since we only know the lit pixel and the source location. We can only deduce the trajectory if we assume the photon traveled in a straight path (the path of least action). But in doing so, we have already assumed that it did not make any turns or explore other pathways.
In this case, we merely disrupted the properties of the mirror by placing something on top of it, altering the angle of reflection.

Edit: No matter what trajectory light is following we will only see one pixel, so point B being lit if we follow the theory. So to prove the theory we need to determine the trajectory followed by the light that hits the same pixel not 2 different ones. One example i think of it would be to block the least action trajectory and still see the same pixel being hit, so basicaly having the light source in an infinite empty space and a sensor. Then putting something that absorbs 100% of the light that hits it blocking the least action trajectory, then disturbing the alternative pathways and as soon as we disturb the alternative pathways our sensor will light up. In the Veritasium experiment the least action trajectory was not blocked. At 29:51 the pixel is supposed to be off yet it is still on so the least action trajectory was not blocked at all.

Author: @JD-ub5ic
Content:
There is a meme going around on reddit where someone does exactly the "cover the reflection" thing you showed here, and when the person goes "how does the camera see my reflection?" they are mocked for being stupid and not understanding "basic" physics. I contend that this video is proof that this idea is MUCH more complicated than the redditors mocking someone for asking questions would have you think, and they don't understand it either. 

First, my elementary understanding would have told me there is only 1 "apparent" image, that is object (person) appearing inside the mirror, and if you cover the cameras perspective you would have to move the observer in order to see that apparent image - it has more to do with geometry than physics. This is usually what they do, they cover the mirror with a blanket and then the camera walks closer to the mirror to show the person holding the blanket, but this experiment showed that you could see the apparent image of the person covering the mirror even without moving the observer/camera - that is completely contrary to my understanding of this and I'm an engineer I like to think I know physics🤣. 

The experiment showed light takes every path which proves that my understanding was wrong, there isn't only 1 apparent image, there's infinitely many, and in order to see the image you don't need to move the observer you simply need to filter out some of the paths to see different apparent images - the camera/observer can stay still. VERY interesting, and further proof of the importance of asking questions and not mocking people for asking questions - it could be that they actually understand far more than you do, enough to ask the question in the first place. Thank you Mr Feynman.

- Discusses how these developments paved the way for the wave nature of particles.
13:11:00 *⚡ De Broglie’s Wave-Particle Duality and Feynman’s Quantum Path Integral*
- De Broglie proposes that matter particles have a wavelength, reinforcing the wave nature of electrons.  
- Feynman’s path integral formulation shows that all possible paths must be considered for quantum calculations.  
- Introduces the idea of adding amplitudes from all paths to calculate quantum events.
16:02:00 *🌠 Quantum Mechanics and the Infinite Slit Experiment*
- Describes the double slit experiment and how the wave function involves all possible paths between two points.  
- Feynman’s interpretation suggests particles explore all paths, including those beyond classical limits, like faster-than-light paths or those going back in time.

20:21:00 *⏳ The Role of Phase and Action in Quantum Mechanics*
- Introduces the concept of phase and how it changes for each path in quantum mechanics.  
- Describes how the action integral determines phase changes and how this leads to constructive or destructive interference.  
- Explains how the tiny value of Planck’s constant results in the cancellation of most quantum paths in macroscopic objects.
24:35 *✨ Path of Least Action and Constructive Interference*
- Explains how paths close to the path of least action constructively interfere, resulting in the observed trajectory.  
- Light and particles explore all paths, but the paths of least action dominate the outcome.  
- Larger particles (e.g., planets, balls) have limited path diversity due to their larger actions, while smaller particles (e.g., electrons) exhibit more varied paths.
26:02 *💡 Experimental Demonstration of Quantum Path Exploration*

29:28 *🔬 Laser Experiment with Path Exploration*

- Demonstrates how, even with laser light, some paths are canceled out while others are amplified.  
- Reinforces the idea that quantum particles (including light) explore all potential paths, and the constructive interference leads to the observable outcome.
31:25 *📐 Action and the Principle of Least Action in Physics*
- Reflects on the importance of action in physics, emphasizing its centrality in theoretical physics over traditional concepts like energy and forces.

Author: @NZ-fo8tp
Content: The comment about the double slit experiment not adhering to locality or universal speed limits is alittle misleading. It’s far more subtle than that to the point that it’s honestly probably better for the average first year physics student to approach the subject with an assumption of locality. Saying that a particle actually physically tried every possible path, based on the successful use of a particular mathematical model to predict empirical data is actually not good physics. The math works on a distribution, a particle is a sample from that distribution. You can do all sorts of math on the distribution you could let it evolve over time with theoretical laws, when you measure a particle you are just sampling the distribution. you need to take a lot of sample before you start seeing the data fit the model distribution. The theory approximates some underlying process that physically applies to particles

Just because QM mathematically implies "every path" it does not follow that every possibility is realized (even if "realized" only applies to the math). I just don't know of a logical approach to prove that the limitations are absolute, and not just a matter of "astronomically low probability".

Author: @Phlosioneer
Content: This doesn’t work as a true explanation for macroscopic particles. It’s the truth but not the whole truth. Macroscopic objects can encounter situations where multiple paths have roughly equivalent action potentials. But they don’t actually take both paths. They take one path. It’s not *enough* for two paths to have very very very similar actions. You also need to include the width, or the std deviation, of the potentials (I will use “width” b/c it’s easier to type). You need to include the width because the real world has random fluctuations; the distributions of two paths must overlap even when those fluctuations occur. For macroscopic objects, the width of the distributions are absurdly tiny. But for particles, the width of the distributions is enough for the paths to interact with each other even when disturbed slightly. And for molecules, their action distributions are usually too small to observe quantum path interactions, but you can sometimes get the conditions just right (particularly in crystals with low temperatures).

Author: @wtfdinges
Content:
I'm highly skeptical of the explanation provided here. While I am not an expert on this particular topic, I do have significant experience working with quantum tunneling and single photon problems. What you are suggesting is that a mathematical solution is the physical answer, which is not necessarily the case. It involves many assumptions, including the fact that light is a particle and a wave. We know it behaves just like a particle when we look at it one way and behaves just like a wave when we look at it another way, but we have no clue how or why. It's even possible that it's a completely different mechanic that we have not yet discovered or don't fully understand and just has some similarities with particles and waves. 

Another problem with this particular explanation is that light would always take the quickest path, regardless of initial direction. In other words: your laser would just skip the mirror and go straight from the source to the camera. This is obviously not the case. It doesn't matter whether that's because of wave theory, because a moving particle with mass requires some external force to change direction, or something else entirely. What does matter is that we simply lack the understanding and are missing some key answers to the question "why?". I'm confident we're slowly getting there, but it appears the answer becomes more complex with every clue we find. Heck, it could be that the answer is at an asymptote of knowledge that we will never be able to fully reach.

That we must consider every possibility is not the same as that it takes every path: it takes the path of least resistance which we cannot know unless we consider every path and what is along that path.

We see the same thing with GPS-navigation, that must consider all possible paths and the more it sends cars down one path the more resistant the path gets and another path is "shorter" in time.

And the fact that the double-slit experiment is claimed to show interference pattern over time with particles shows that something is not explained by the quantum explanation, because the waves alternate between a positive value and a negative one with the zero nodes in-between, whereas particle counts are always absolute magnitudes above zero so there is no interference in the values themselves, but they would have to be proportional to the square of the wave if they're related at all.

However, if you've ever created a 'camera obscura' with multiple holes, it is the same image interfering with itself over and over again rather than single photons.

Content: 33:36 The camera we are watching through is picking up the internal reflections from the laser emitter directly (you can see the laser he is holding as well as the projection on the card). If you want to make an experiment to actually confirm the theory, you need a truly black room and emitter, and a polarizing filter at the receiving end. You then would turn the polarizer to detect different phases of the same laser source reflected off a "perfectly" smooth mirror with the position varying together with the phase to show the alternate paths. Content:
30:20 we can see a red dot at the laser source, which means the laser is also emitting light directly into the camera. There is stray light and this is an imperfect set up. 

If you shine a laser through a single slit of a double slit experiment, you won't see interference.

The "exploring all paths" is a mathematical artifact. The effects can all be explained by a wave function and its equations. Those are partial differential equations that can be discretized and calculated with only neighboring contributions. This is a fact that is easily checked by looking at the Schrödinger equation.


It is true that the path integral is an alternative way of making calculations but it does not necessarily reflect reality in the sense that something real actually travels everywhere.

Author: @martymoo
Content:
I think it's important to emphasise that the path integral formalism does not imply that a photon "chooses" a path and then discards others. Instead, it describes how all paths contribute to the final probability amplitude.

I would also highlight that while individual paths are not observed directly, their contributions collectively determine measurable outcomes. The integral over all possible paths is not just a mathematical trick -- it reflects physical reality. In reality, quantum particles do not follow a single classical trajectory. Instead, they interfere with themselves as if taking all paths.

To clarify further: the wave function describes a superposition of all possible paths, and the probability distribution is an intrinsic feature of quantum mechanics, not just an epistemic limitation (restriction on knowledge).

Author: @thenorthernclouds
Content:
Even lasers have scattered light. This scattered light is of course very weak, but it is easy to recognise in the dark. And of course this scattered light is then visible from the camera due to refraction at the grid. If Feynman's theory were correct, individual sharp points should not appear under these conditions, but rather a washed-out pattern. 
I could also prove that it is scattered light. If you were to place a mirror instead of the grating at an angle of approx. 45° to the plane of the table, you would also see a red dot in this mirror in the dark, which is caused by the scattered light from the laser. 
So the experiment does not show that Feynman's theory is correct. on the contrary, the pattern that can be seen actually contradicts this theory. So it is rather a refutation of Feynman's theory.

Author: @gryyphyn8639
Content: that proof of a laser appearing on the diffraction film is easily explained by the emission at the source not being truly linear. Lasers, especially cheap ones but all lasers in general, do NOT release all light in a perfectly linear manner. That is not to say that their light takes a path other than the "laser straight" beam, that is to say that they have non-linear emission from the source due to imperfections in the optics and emitter shielding. If you look at a laser source, especially one very close to the emission source, you'll see a scattered pattern of dots. Author: @kfftfuftur
Content:
I'm not convinced that your experiments prove that light takes all possible paths. The way I see it, photons are emitted as individual waves which can spread out over some region of space. Each photon can only explore those regions that are covered by it's wave function. I think it is important to realize that only very few of the photons emitted by the lamp are able to reach the camera. Some of the photons happen to be emitted in the correct direction to be reflected into the camera and some other photons are emitted in the correct direction to be refracted into the camera by the diffraction grating. Both paths exist independently so covering up the reflection of the lamp won't make the photons find another path to the camera.

If you have photons that are only emitted in the direction to be reflected into the camera they won't produce an image in the diffraction grating. The reason you still see one with the laser pointer is that it also emits stray light that was scattered by imperfections or dust on the lens. That's why you can still see that the laser pointer is on when it isn't directly pointed at the camera. Only this stray light is able to reach the diffraction grating.

While watching the video I was instead expecting you to talk about the Aharonov Bohm effect where electrons are affected by the presence of a magnetic field in a region of space that they are unable to reach.

Content: Once you read "Feynmans Quantum Path Integrals" it all gets clear. You can even use them to derive Schroedingers equation. The "spooky" thing is: this does not only apply for space but also for time - including the future. A possible interaction in the future influences the presence, as those "path" interacting with future also add to the action NOW. So the possibility of an interaction in the future DOES indeed change the presence. In a predicable (computable) way and also measurably. E.g. if you have an atom in an excited state and look at the probability of it spontaneously falling back into the ground state it is influenced by the possibility that the photon, emitted at  the transition from the excited to the ground state, will be captured after is has been emitted causing the atom to go back to the excited state. This future possibility actually does increase the probability of the spontaneous transition from excited to ground state. This has been computed and measured and both agree - for an effect that changes the probability by 1e-10! So the whole idea of causality - the presence is only influenced by things that happened in the past - is wrong. The possible interactions in the "future" do change the presence! If you can not sleep after reading this - don't worry: you'll accept it some day.

Everytime this piece of pseudo history shows up. Here's the correct order of events:
Rayleigh's black body (BB) equation was published in June 1900. Planck, without knowing Rayleigh's result, published his BB equation in October 1900. Content:
I'm not doubting the theory but the final experiment doesn't seem to work for me... that sheet he lays down, with whatever tiny geometries are inside of it, is simply changing the angle the light hits them and is reflected in a different direction, toward the camera. Now I know he addresses this obvious objection with the laser experiment, but I think this is also potentially flawed.  You can easily observe this yourself... if you have a cheap laser, and you're in the dark, let someone else hold the laser and turn it on but with it not pointing at your eyes.  For his experiment here to be valid, based on the notion that the laser is classically believed to truly only be going in one direction, then you should not see the laser turn on when looking at it, if it's not pointed at your eyes.  But we all know that you CAN indeed see when someone turns on a laser pointer even if it's not pointed directly at your eyes.  But this in itself doesn't prove that light is travelling in all directions, it just proves that our lenses and optics aren't perfect... the front glass or lens of the laser diffracts/diffuses the light to some small measurable degree, so we can see red light when it turns on, but it is dim compared to if it was pointed at our eyes.

Now perhaps if we put a tube at the end of the laser such that we could not see the lens or glass cover at the end of the laser directly at all, but only the open end of the tube, and if the inside of this tube was as close to a black body as possible, absorbing all the light that had been diffracted/diffused and was going in all directions, then we should expect to see nothing, and if we did see nothing, THEN this experiment could be performed with this new laser contraption and if a reflection was STILL picked up by the camera then the point would be proven.  Only with a laser pointed through a black tube like this could we expect with high level conventional understanding that all the laser light was moving purely in one direction, rather than 99.99% moving in one direction but .001% having been diffracted/diffused and going in all directions, which we all clearly see any time someone turns on a laser pointer and we see it turn on even when it's not pointed at us.

Author: @ihrbekommtmeinenrichtigennamen
Content:
30:16 Assuming that the laser is a point-source a certain distance away from a flat surface: At the point that's closest to the source, the light hits with a certain phase. As you go further away from that point, the distance between the source and surface increases. This is radially symmetric. At some point the distance will have increased by one wavelength of the source's light. The radius of that ring is √((height + some integer * wavelength)² - height²). At 650nm (which is probably what this red laser outputs) and (what I judge to be approximately) half a meter distance between the laser and the table, that first ring has a radius of ~0.8mm, the second ring ~1.1mm, etc. Theoretically, the spacing gets closer and closer to 650nm as you approach infinite distance.

If you want the lines in the foil to interact with those areas of same-phase light, the line-spacing would ideally be equal to the ring-spacing, but a small variation should be fine. My gut feeling tells me that the effect gradually decreases to 0 as you get to a factor of 2. So at 1000 lines per mm line-spacing, the ring-spacing would need to be like anywhere from ~700 to ~1400 to get a reasonable effect.
If you count up how many rings fit within two given distances, that gives you a good approximation of how many lines per mm you need in that area. Here are some numbers:

      3 rings fit between a radius of  1.8 and 2.2   mm ->    ~7 lines/mm
     15 rings fit between a radius of  4.5 and 5.5   mm ->   ~15 lines/mm
     62 rings fit between a radius of    9 and  11   mm ->   ~31 lines/mm
    246 rings fit between a radius of   18 and  22   mm ->   ~61 lines/mm
   1530 rings fit between a radius of   45 and  55   mm ->  ~153 lines/mm
   6033 rings fit between a radius of   90 and 110   mm ->  ~301 lines/mm
  22841 rings fit between a radius of  180 and 220   mm ->  ~571 lines/mm
 108649 rings fit between a radius of  450 and 550   mm -> ~1086 lines/mm
 274987 rings fit between a radius of  900 and 1100  mm -> ~1374 lines/mm
 596844 rings fit between a radius of 1800 and 2200  mm -> ~1492 lines/mm
1530750 rings fit between a radius of 4500 and 5500  mm -> ~1530 lines/mm
3073045 rings fit between a radius of 9000 and 11000 mm -> ~1536 lines/mm

So you reach the 1000 lines per millimeter of the foil around half a meter (or ~45°) over, which is approximately where the laser is directly pointed at this setup. Let's start with an even simpler thought experiment. What is happening right before an electron is even emitted in a double slit experiment?  I'd expect that as the device charged up (or reached the peak of its emission cycle), the entire area apparatus it would become polarized (even if pure vacuum).  If you don't take this into account when you try to analyze the results, you will get "mysterious" behavior. The description of the electron in the Standard Model is pretty much nonsense. The best way to explain it is that it is like a storm - it has no point, it is a swirling effect.  When there is only 1 slit, the storm, to conserve angular moment, can only pass straight through.  But as soon as you add a second slit, the arms of the storm will find 1 slit before the other (most of the time) and you will get an interference pattern over time.

Or, to emphasize even more, the electron is non-local, it reaches out to influence the entire system at once.  And this is true of every other atom / molecule / particle in the system.

You may say this is "nonsense", but it's what J.C. Maxwell believed and still no one understands his original equations or their full implications.  For one thing, they allow for an electromagnetic wave to get trapped in loop of its own creation.

Author: @steffenbendel6031
Content:
The laser light interpretation is not entirely correct. In the video you can see the exit point of the laser beam, because there the light is diffracted (and it is not a part of the 'laser beam' anymore). And that diffracted light then creates the pattern when getting diffracted on the grid. The pure laser beam would not do that. Because a laser beam has a phase structure goes to zero if you go away from the center of the beam.. And in Feynman infinite nested path integrals you can neglect all paths that go through points where the sum of all amplitude of all paths is zero. You end up with a Schroedinger (like) equation that is far more smooth and simple to understand. The path integral is just an unnecessary overblown formulation of it (because in some way you introduce the sum of infinities that are zero). 
If you want laser light to spread out, you have to block part of the laser beam (like with a pin hole or a slit or just blocking one side of it) that keeps it focussed.

Author: @AmarantiStellar
Content:
I tend to think of particles as being squishy.  You smoosh the particle across spacetime but its still one object, just smooshed.  Until it interacts with something strongly enough which forces the particle to exist exclusively at the location of that interaction.  After which it starts smooshing out again.

This is why light always takes the shortest path.  Because the shortest path, by definition, will be the first thing it interacts with strongly enough to force it to unsmoosh.  All the possible paths the photon could have taken, are in a race together to see who reaches a major interaction first, and there can only be one winner: whatever turned put to be the shortest path.

The "squishy particle" metaphor falls apart a little when you realize it can be squished in a way where there are two disconnected parts with nothing in-between, and yet despite that they still remain as a single object.  But if you can accept that bit of quantum weirdness, "squishy particles" metaphor makes most of the rest of quantum stuff less weird.

Author: @philosopherhobbs
Content:
This good video is a bad argument. The argument starts from the assumption that an electron goes through both or many slits and the conclusion is that it must also go through infinite slits. Not only is that not super surprising but not every interpretation of QM will grant the initial assumption (which is seemingly absurd that an electron could go through both slits). Other interpretations will say something completely different is going on from the beginning. In many worlds, the electron goes through only 1 slit but there are infinite worlds in each of which it goes through a different slit/path. In pilot wave theory the infinite paths are just epistemic possibilities because we don't know the positions of the particles to start with. Small variations in starting positions can result in very different outcomes because of the wave. This latter view isn't puzzling at all; afterall, we in fact don't know the initial positions and objects don't ever seem to be in multiple places at the same time. Seems like pilot wave theory just gives the most obvious and boring explanation.

Likewise, the laser experiment doesn't show that any single particle is taking all possible paths. It only shows that some of the particles take different paths. What reason is given will vary according to the interpretation of QM favored.

Author: @StevenLovegrove
Content: I love your channel and this video, but the experiment at the end is in my opinion not so conclusive and can be explained by classic wave optics that could be replicated in waves in water just as the double slit experiment could be. The intuition presented is that a laser sends all of its energy in a straight line, but a laser has an approximately Gaussian transverse beam profile and you can detect photons significantly off-axis. You can observe this directly by the fact the end of a laser pointer appears to glow even when not pointed directly at you, demonstrating how it's energy is distributed over a wider angle (though mostly concentrated forward). Instead of a diffraction grating, you could place a white piece of paper off-axis and you would still detect slightly increased photon count from the paper on the CCD due to diffuse scattering towards the camera. The effect of the diffraction grating is to concentrate the integral of energy collected from the grating into certain directions through the resultant interference wave (in the far field), hence making it easier to observe as more concentrated dots on the CCD. I.e., you could still explain the phenomena with a local wave equation. It doesn't get really funky until you start using a single photon source where you would presumably still observe interference. I'm not a physicist, so I come from a place of good intention, interest and some ignorance, but the path integral formulation feels to me like an alternative but equivalent view of Fresnel wave propagation? All that said, I really like the presentation and how it illuminates possible underlying realities! Thanks for making such great videos and making us all think a little harder!

Author: @marciodasb5189
Content: You're presenting the Copenhagen interpretation as if it were an objective fact, but it's just one possible way to interpret quantum mechanics. Saying 'the particle goes through both slits at the same time' is an assumption based on superposition, but alternative interpretations (like Bohmian mechanics) describe a definite path instead. Likewise, claiming that 'every particle must take all possible paths' only holds under Feynman’s path integral formulation—it’s a mathematical tool, not necessarily a physical reality. Please acknowledge the different interpretations instead of pushing Copenhagen as the absolute truth.

Author: @josephkahr74
Content: The amplitudes at point B can sum only if they arrive at the same time.  Rather than have many in-sync "clocks" starting at point A at the same time and traveling along various paths of different lengths, one can have one clock at point A sending out a continuous sine wave of amplitudes.  The amplitude of each wave front is constant as it travels from A to B.  To have wave fronts from all paths arrive at B at the same time each must leave A one travel time earlier, depending on its A to B path.  The amplitude delivered from A to B depends on the path length, same as the traveling clock picture, but with the necessary superposition of wave fronts at B.  This implies that all relevant paths must start at A within a time range when the continuous wave is coherent, otherwise the amplitudes at B would be chaotic and tend to wash out.

Author: @marcobiagini1878
Content:
My name is Marco Biagini and I am a physicist; I would like to explain the “observation” problem in quantum mechanics because it is often misunderstood even by many physicists. 
In quantum mechanics the state of a physical system is described by the wave function and does not have defined values ​​for all the physical quantities measurable on it; on the other hand, only the probability distributions relating to the measurable values ​​for these quantities are defined. Once the measurement has been carried out, the system will have a defined value in relation to the measured quantity, and this involves a radical modification of its wave function; in fact the wave function generally describes infinite possibilities while for an event to take place, it is necessary that the wave function assigns a probability of 100% to a single possibility and 0% probability to all the others. If all other results are not eliminated by imposing the collapse "by hand" on the wave function, the predictions of subsequent measurements on the same system will be wrong. The transition between a state that describes many possibilities to a state that describes only one possibility is called “collapse of the wave function”. The time evolution of the wave function is determined by Schrödinger's equation, but this equation never determines the collapse of the wave function, which instead is imposed by the physicist "by hand"; the collapse represents a violation of the Schrödinger equation, and the cause of the collapse is therefore attributable only to an agent not described by the Schrödinger equation itself.  The open problem in  quantum physics is that the cause of the transition between the indeterminate state and the determined state, cannot be traced back to any physical interaction, because all known physical interactions are already included in the Schrödinger's equation; in fact,  the collapse of the wave function is a violation of the Schrodinger's equation, i.e. a violation of the most fundamental laws of physics and therefore the cause of the collapse cannot be determined by the same laws of physics, in particular, it cannot be determined by the interactions already included in the Schrodinger's equation. 

After one century of debates, the problem of measurement in quantum mechanics is still open and still represents the crucial problem for all interpretations of quantum mechanics. In fact, on the one hand it represents a violation of the Schrodinger equation, that is, a violation of the fundamental laws of physics. On the other hand, it is necessary for the laws of quantum physics to make sense, and to be applied in the interpretation and prediction of the phenomena we observe. Indeed, since the wave function represents infinite possibilities, without the collapse there would be no event; for there to be an event, then there must be one possibility that is actualized by canceling all other possibilities.
This is the inescapable contradiction against which, all attempts to reconcile quantum physics with realism, break. 

Quantum mechanics does not describe reality as something that exists objectively at every instant, but as a collection of events isolated in time (i.e. the phenomena we observe at the very moment in which we observe them), while among these events there are only infinite possibilities and there is no continuity between events. 

In fact, the properties of a physical system are determined only after the collapse of the wave function; when the properties of the system are not yet determined, the system is not real, but only an idea, a hypothesis. Only when collapse occurs do properties become real because they take on a definite value.  It makes no sense to assume that the system exists but its properties are indeterminate, because properties are an intrinsic aspect of the system itself; for example, there can be no triangle with indeterminate sides and no circle with indeterminate radius. People often say that a quantum particle is in many places at the same time but this is just an absurd interpretation since it implies logical contradictions; a non-collapsed wave function describes infinite possibilities and not a particle that occupies infinite positions at the same time. 
If the  properties are indeterminate it means that such properties do not exist which implies that the system itself does not exist; actually photons, electrons and quantum particles in general are just the name we give to some mathematical equations. The collapse represents the transition from infinite hypothetical possibilities to an actual event.

Quantum mechanics is therefore incompatible with realism (that's why Einstein never accepted quantum mechanics) and all attempts to reconcile quantum mechanics with realism are flawed. Since the collapse of the wave function violates the fundamental laws of physics, it  can only be associated with an agent that is not described by the Schrodinger equation, and the only event we know of that is irreducible to the Schrodinger equation is consciousness. Therefore, events can only exist when consciousness is involved in the process; contrary to what many claim, a measuring instrument cannot cause the collapse of the wave function.

However, the fact that properties are created when a conscious mind observes the system in no way implies that it is the observer or his mind that creates those properties and causes the collapse; I regard this hypothesis as totally unreasonable (by the way, the universe is supposed to have existed even before the existence of humans). The point is that there must be a correlation between the existence of an event (associated to the collapse of the wave function =violation of the physical laws) and the interaction with a non-physical agent (the human mind); however, correlation does not mean causation because the concomitance of two events does not imply a causal link. 

No cause of collapse is necessary in an idealistic perspective, which assumes that there is no mind-independent physical reality and that physical reality exists as a concept in the mind of God that directly creates the phenomena we observe in our mind (any observed phenomenon is a mental experience) ; the collapse of the wave function is only a representation of God's act of creation in our mind of the observed phenomenon and is an element of the algorithm we have developed to make predictions and describe the phenomena we observe. This is essentially the view of the Irish philosopher George Berkeley, and in this view God is not only the Creator, but also the Sustainer of the universe.  The fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics is that reality is not described as a continuum of events but as isolated events, and this is in perfect agreement with the idealistic view which presupposes that what we call "universe" is only the set of our sensory perceptions and that the idea that an external physical reality exists independently of the mind is only the product of our imagination; in other words, the universe is like a collective dream created by God in our mind. Idealism provides the only logically consistent interpretation of quantum mechanics, but most physicists do not accept idealism because it contradicts their personal beliefs, so they prefer an objectively wrong interpretation that gives them the illusion that quantum mechanics is compatible with realism.
