Author: @hellohi2516
Content:
Something about that laser experiment at 30:13 bothers me, at least in comparison to the open bulb. The wide-view camera is able to see the end of the laser even though it’s not pointing at it, meaning the laser is still scattering light. It isn’t a perfect laser, so it isn’t really that different than the lightbulb experiment. If you add a shroud around the end of the laser, obstructing the glass at the end that is scattering the light, would the experiment still work?


That was my main concern, but I do have some other thoughts that I also can’t work out, and I figure I should write them in this comment as well:

In a perfect vacuum, with a perfect laser and a perfect mirror, would this experiment still work? Suppose the laser turns electricity into completely mono-directional light with 100% efficiency and the mirror is able to reflect the entire luminosity of the laser without any scattering or absorption. On the other end, our observer is a perfect black sensor, able to absorb 100% of the photons and display that energy. We then perform the experiment (assuming the paper is also perfectly black). Would the sensor still observe the new reflection? How much luminosity could it have? If we then take the paper away, but leave the diffraction grating, would the original reflection still be visible and would it have the same luminosity? If that were true, wouldn’t the sensor now show more energy input than the laser is outputting?

In my opinion, the above scenario could be feasible only if the action of blocking certain pathways (by placing the grating) decreases the original reflection’s luminosity. Considering what we see in the real world, I can’t imagine that that decrease is significant. I think the change would be infinitesimally small, and therefore the second reflection would be infinitesimally bright, which leads me to believe the real world experiment may not be a good example of the actual phenomenon, as the luminosity of the second reflection seems to be from light that is scattered by the glass on the laser to that point on the mirror, not light that originally was visible in the reflection exploring alternate pathways. It might still demonstrate the path of least action, just not in as rigorous a scenario as the experiment claims.

Another concern I had was with the assertion that in order to explain the double slit experiment, we have to think of each photon as taking both paths. Couldn’t the same phenomenon be explained by many photons taken in aggregate? The probabilities would emerge as a phenomenon of large numbers, with the interference being between different photons, not a single photon with itself. That would also explain how longer paths “break” the speed of light. If different photons are emitted at different times, they can arrive at the same time by traveling the same speed along different paths. The fact that they took different times to go different paths explains why they can be out of phase and can destructively interfere.

In a way, it could be compared to a Galton board. The end result shows the probability of a single marble falling in a specific slot, yet if you observe a single marble, it still only takes a single path.

One question that may actually be evidence of the least action principle I’ve had a hard time finding the answer to. How can the bending of the light during diffraction be explained without having the photons explore every possible path and choose the ones with least action? I know that light is a wave, which is what the experiment originally was trying to demonstrate, but generally, the electromagnetic wave is shown as something stable that travels in a single direction, always perpendicular to the transverse fluctuations. This is in contrast with something like sound, for example, which propagates and diffuses as it travels, since the kinetic energy can split among the particles of the medium. Sound going through a slit would propagate in all directions as the pressure fluctuates, each particle pushing into multiple neighbors, spreading out like ripples on the surface of water. Can photons moving in the same direction also do that when passing through a slit? Light can be emitted in many directions or be scattered by particles, but as far as I know, in the interim, each photons travels in a straight line. So what changes when it passes through a slit?

All this said, it’s not that I don’t believe the theory is true, I just like to understand where the classical explanation breaks down. I don’t really feel satisfied with these experiments and their explanations.

Author: @jmcsquared18
Content:
I love this topic, just finished this unit in undergraduate modern physics. It's so much fun showing students the history of how these early quantum ideas arose. 

One interesting detail, Planck did *not* introduce the quantum of light. He believed that the atoms in the blackbody constituted little oscillators that vibrated with energies nhf and none in between. Einstein's interpretation of Planck's blackbody formula as photons - light particles - was initially rejected by the entire physics community.

Contrary to what is often explained in physics courses, even Planck himself didn't believe Einstein. In his recommendation to the Prussian academy, Planck said of Einstein, "that he may sometimes have *missed the target* in his speculations, as, for example, in his hypothesis of *light quanta*, cannot really be held too much against him." 

Then Robert Millikan tried to prove Einstein wrong and ended up doing a photoelectric experiment in 1914 so good that proved him completely correct. The history of early quantum theory is mostly people making ridiculous proposals that experts thought were so crazy that they tried to disprove them, only to give the proposals perfect confirmation.

Author: @andrzejr82
Content:
I am always disappointed with science communicators that they can't explain this subject properly. They always talk about "when light travels from A to B through a density boundary, it chooses the optimal path". But that is meaningless. A photon doesn't sit there, planning his journey to a pre-determined point B that lies somewhere in a different medium, and then based on some calculations in its tiny photon mind picks the shortest path. A photon is just fired by the light source in some direction and travels in a straight line until it hits a new medium under an angle. Because of the density difference, it changes the angle, and happens to end up in B. If it left the light source traveling in a different direction, it would just not end up in B. In what sense then is the light "choosing" the shortest path? It's the person holding the laser pointer at point A that chooses to illuminate point B and it's that person who fiddles with the angle of the laser until it illuminates point B. The light didn't choose anything.

I've never seen or heard or read a proper explanation of what scientists mean here when they're talking about light making choices, and until someone does explain it, this video (and the previous one about action) will not make any sense to me.

I hope Veritasium reads this comment and makes a video about this, because it really seems to me like a huge flaw in the foundation of what he's trying to explain.

Author: @tekchip
Content:
Isn't this just classic physics? A sort of pressure wave preceding a particle? The wave begets the path the particle takes? Like a ball floating on water or air particles being pushed ahead of physical objects. The math just seems to be proving what we already know but didn't expect to see at such an incredible small scale. Sort of classic physics but inverse because we're coming at it from big instead of coming at it from small. The experiment at the end is just showing that a handful of light particles are sort of straying off the path the waves beget. You dump a bunch of balls in a pond and make waves and majority of balls will adhere to the standing wave pattern but some will still stray due to contact with other things, variation in viscosity etc. etc. No matter how strong you make the waves (laser) there are always outside, uncalculated, forces that cause some straying. Literal path of least resistance as "explored" by the waves preceding the particle. Which seems like a misnomer. Are we able to measure the speed of wave vs the speed of particle? When a light comes on do the waves reach the point we expect to see the particle first? I'd wager we can't, yet, but when we can we'll find wave precedes particle by some insanely small difference in speed.

Thinking about it further and re-watching the video a Quantum isn't "action" whatever that is. It's simply a variable for yet unknown speed of waves. The speed of the light is the speed of particle, but we don't yet know the speed of wave. So we've called it quantum right? We plug in action beside the speed of particle and it works. So h becomes some number once we figure out how to measure it the way we've measured the speed of light particles.

Author: @MoeOuan666
Content:
Hum.....Not really convinced, not that Hamiltonian formulation with actions in the configuration space is wrong or not a powerful mathematical tool...What I am not convinced is that it is a fundamental description of what really happen (in a causal sense), and not a math recast using optimisation/integration  formalism...Why? Because even doing a proper simulation of newtonian mechanic using particles, or of fluid/waves using latice boltzmann (a crude approx of molecules), you get something that can be predicted using an action formalism. Except that contrary to reality (where ultimately QM muddle everything), there you are absolutely sure deep down it's just a causal local interactions (quasi-newtonian collisions and interaction forces for particles, or a lattice update akin cellular automata) because you programmed it. So I believe it's the same for reality: Hamiltonian in phase-space is a nice mathematical tool, not the way things really happen in the world. For classic mechanics, for GR and for QM (see Jacob Barandes as QM interpretation that is much closer to classical mechanics than an action minimisation in phase space abstraction).
An example on why I think causality does not play nice with the action: light indeed takes the shortest path...knowing already emission and reception point. If there actually is some kind of optimisation going on, how do you know the reception point at emission time? So, like classical formulation of GR and path integrals in QM, it's a block-time view of the universe, the future and the past actually exists, it's not even clear what the present is. Or it's you get your optimisation through a variant of multi-world? Both seems very dubious to me...more dubious than local interpretation writing classical wave propagation equations.
The laser was impressive....except I have the impression what you see is the diffracted (by the diffraction network) image of laser leakage out of the main beam. If it's the case, much less impressive because it's exactly the same as for the classic lamp -- except laser leak image are more clearly separated because light is more monochromatic). It's not that clear in the video, but if you can see the leakage in the mirror (with your eyes or moving the camera) without the diffraction network sheet, bingo....and I think it's the case, replaying the section when  laser was moved around.
laser leakage  is the  light you see looking at a laser out of the main beam. It's weak but not that weak in the absolute sense....just weak compared to the main beam, which is literally blinding (never look at it)

Author: @TejasIsAmazing
Content:
I was kind of "iffy" about the last demo due to the spillage of light at 30:15, so after pondering about it for a while, i have come to some understandings. I am not a physicist, nor have i studied this physics, so i am probably wrong, and if so, please correct me.

The spilling of light is necessary here to even see the reflection from the foil. If you were able to reduce this spilling, you would be dramatically increase the action of the photons along the path which goes towards the foil. And then via the division by the small "h" idea, the phase would be essentially random again, and you wouldn't see the light on the foil due to the cancellations. Increasing the "resolution" of the foil should again be able to show the light due to more precision on removing half of the phases or something, but you can only do this to a limit. At approaching 0 spilling, aka the light traveling exactly straight out of the laser, the action of every other path would be approaching infinity, and thus we would only see the laser follow its normal trajectory, and we would not see anything on the foil.

This is also why you wouldn't really see the light on the foil if the foil was in another room. The action would be so large, that you just would not be able to make a fine enough film to remove the correct phase of the action.

Another thing tho, since if the spilling is required, we can also just think of it without action, as if the photons are already going to the place the foil was placed at, due to the spilling. They just are not very visible initially, because its not a lot of photons, and they are reflected in essentially a random direction. Adding the foil adds diffraction into the picture, which due to the wave nature of light, causes it to constructively and destructively interfere in certain spots and angles based on wavelength, which is what we see as the several points of light on the foil, instead of just one. So basically, this experiment doesn't really "prove" the action model.

And this should not really be unexpected. The principle of least action is not really predicting anything new, its just giving a different interpretation/frameworks to existing models. Both the photon+wave model and the least action are predicting the same thing for light, just in different ways. The principle of least action is more like a general framework for physics, its not really new physics i think?

What is unexpected and kinda beautiful to me tho, is how the least action works out to be such a general principle and applicable basically everywhere.

Content:
One of my wonders in physics is how deeply mathematics connects with the physical universe. It’s interesting that many physics learners end up treating math merely as a tool to quantify phenomena, often overlooking its qualitative insights. When we do that, we sometimes miss what the underlying mathematical structure is really emphasizing. There are plenty of examples of this.
Take, for instance, when Max Planck solved the ultraviolet catastrophe by assuming the quantization of electromagnetic radiation. Similarly, when Einstein’s theory hinted at an expanding universe, he was skeptical at first.

Author: @TiSapph
Content:
The implication of laser experiment is incorrect, what you are seeing the scatter from the laser module. It is exactly the same as the lamp, it is not showing that the laser beam itself takes paths across the foil. That's why the laser spot on the card moves, while the spot on the foil doesn't much.
The issue is that the "explores all paths and finds the minimum" argument assumes you are starting from a single point-like location. Photons from the laser are spread over the entire output beam cross-section, with the same phase everywhere in the cross-section. To get a bright spot somewhere, paths from *all locations* on the output cross-section need to add up. The maths works out to a beam which slowly expands. The smaller the output beam, the stronger the divergence. For a tiny output beam, the beam is more of a cone, approaching the model of a point-like source.
So for any location which is not on the beam, the waves already destructively interfere anyway. The foil doesn't undo that.
The number of incorrect examples in Veritasium videos is getting annoying. There are more than enough astounding real effects that can be shown.

Author: @justrichard2491
Content: I know that this is simply equivocation, because my objection to this video is mostly an objection to the metaphor utilized.  Light, and energy, don't "explore" all pathways to some destination.  Energy doesn't have a destination in mind.  It doesn't have a mind.  It has no agency.  So, it is not exploring all possible pathways to point B.  Rather, it should be obvious that if we can see a photon from all angles relative to its motion, some energy is being emitted in all directions.  And, as energy moves into a new medium, the pathway of least resistance is the direction that the majority of the energy will take.  It is lightning on a smaller scale, except, it is just trying to move along the path of least resistance.  And for light, that means not changing direction.  But, it is also a particle of energy, so it must be emitting energy in all directions as it moves along.  So, I'm not buying the cancellation theory.  That the formulas work is due to the constant, which in my opinion is related to our size relative to the size of atoms.

Author: @bootes3321
Content:
I can't comment on the validity of the underlying principles discussed in the video, but the laser light demonstration does not actually remove the variable of stray light interacting with the diffraction grating. 

At 30:15 you can very clearly see the laser pointer in the dark room (to the left of Casper's head in the main camera angle, not the experiment camera angle), even though the beam is directed at the black sheet on the table. There's enough light leaking out of the side of the laser's front lens to cause camera lens flare. 

The lenses and mirrors inside the laser pointer are not perfect, so extraneous reflections and diffractions occur before the light has even left the laser pointer. In the same way the very expensive camera lens experiences lens flare at 30:15, you can imagine that the cheap laser pointer lens is also experiencing lens flare. 

With the laser acting as a more diffuse light source than suggested in the video, it will of course act in exactly the same way as the flashlight. This gives us the expected result of reflections off of the diffusion grating. 

Now if you put a sheath around the end of the laser pointer coated in something like vantablack, and did the whole experiment in a vacuum, then maaybe we'd be able to see the effects of the infinite paths of light. But honestly the whole premise of this video really feels like putting the cart before the horse by assuming that the light must find a path from point A to point B and therefore all paths must be explored. It really feels like we've moved away from the Occam's Razor approach to assume that light is traveling along a path "that happens when light obeys local rules" like Derek said at 2:08.

Each photon only took one spacetime path, but this can wind about all over the place. The interference effect is from single photons. That's self-entanglement, or vacuum entanglement if you prefer.  You notice the intensity dramatically dims. The photon has an amplitude for going one of many ways, but still most of them hit the cardboard blocker.  It is thus a _stochastic_ effect of entanglement that you are seeing. The path integral or Sum-over-histories is a tool for computing the effects of that entanglement with the vacuum. The single photon does not literally take all paths. If it happened to hit the black line on the grating it is absorbed, no interference amplitude then from _that_ photon, but this cannot possibly interfere with the next photon emitted.
     The _real_ mystery however is entanglement. Entanglement is _why_ the SOH methods works.

Author: @tobiassander3995
Content:
It's a great video, as usual! 
But PLEASE, stop propagating the silly falsehood that many different outcomes *happen* or *exist* at the same time in quantum mechanics. This has become a popular lore, but it is completely and manifestly false. Instead, many different outcomes all *have probabilities* of happening. It really is this simple to clear up a lot of the confusion and supposed mystery of quantum mechanics. 
Let me illustrate this with a simple (classical) example. Suppose a stock is worth $100 today and it may be $105 or $95 (or some other value) tomorrow. Would you say it is worth *both* $105 and $95 simultaneously? Of course, nobody would ever make this silly claim. Instead we say that there are *certain probabilities* for these *different possible outcomes*, and we won't know which one materializes until we see it. It's exactly the same in quantum mechanics.

Author: @Redingold
Content:
"But you have to restrict it to be local, right?"

"The maths doesn't do that"

In non-relativistic quantum mechanics, sure, but when you include special relativity (and end up with quantum field theory) you explicitly do have to account for locality, which is done using Heaviside step functions and what are called time-ordered exponentials to suppress any interactions that occur outside of a particle's past and future light cone (actually, it's more complicated than that, in QFT path integrals are not integrals over the motion of a single particle, they're integrals over all possible configurations of the entire quantum field).

Content: i would like to correct you about how easily you wrote different lagrangians for electrodynamics, General relativity etc. The thing is that variable of integral changes too in action, for example in non relativistic mechanics the variable of integration is time. But in relativity, time becomes a coordinate itself and you integrate over curve parameter say lambda. The second problem with action is that even though we know it works but we don't know how to write its form in a given physical regime. You cannot cook up action until you know the equations of motion. For example you know about maxwell's eqn and then you can create action in form of the field tensor F. But there is no way to formulate action without knowing maxwell equations. So even though action principle works it doesn't tell you how particle will behave in a setup, you need to know it's equation of motion from some other method and then compute the action.

Author: @thehobbyist2431
Content:
The experiment at 30:12 has some flaws and does not really convince me. 
1. Light spillage on the output pupil of the laser pointer. A tupe could help to minimize stray light.
2. The laser shining on the black cardboard. This produces a diffuse reflection and an interference field. It would be better to point the laser on the mirror at an angle that it misses the camera.
3. The mirrior. This seema to be a standard household mirror with the reflective coating in the backside. This leads to internal reflections. Better to use a high qualiti mirror with coating on the front. And use two separate mirrors, one that is directly hit ba the laser beam and the other with the grating on top.
4. The environment. It needs a more controlled environment to make sure there are no unwanded backreflections e.g. from the walls.

If one could repeat this experiment in an actual optics lab with high quality gear, taking into account the points listed above, this would be great.

Author: @changbadinesh
Content:
@veritasium
Fermat's Principle, which claims that light takes the path of least time, seems fundamentally flawed when critically analyzed. Light, being an inanimate phenomenon, cannot "choose" its path or make decisions to optimize travel time. In reality, the path in the first medium is fixed, as the light ray emerges from the source in a straight line and cannot alter its direction. It is only at the interface where refraction occurs, and the bending of light is dictated by the properties of the media. This bending can completely change the target point, not just the path, making it clear that the principle is not about intentional optimization. Introducing an intermediate medium demonstrates how the "target" can shift entirely, proving that Fermat's Principle is more of a coincidental result of physical laws than a deliberate optimization of the path. It describes an outcome but does not fundamentally explain the mechanics of refraction, making its interpretation as a governing law seem superficial and misleading.

25:00 The exact same thing happens with a path of maximal action, if it exists.

I think an important bit omitted here is that any locally stationary point has a zero derivative.

If someone is reading this and the above is Chinese: if you are at the lowest point of something, every direction leads up (or at least none leads down). A ball placed there doesn't roll, it behaves similar to sitting on a perfectly even/horizontal plate. That is meant by "in first order approximation (the plate) it doesn't change (even height)".

The same isn't just true for the lowest point however. It is also true for the highest point (every direction leads down), and it's enough if it is lowest or highest in a small area, not necessarily overall. And there are even more options, like "saddle points" where one side goes up, the other goes down, but you can still place a tiny ball that doesn't roll because the slope vanishes at this point.

Author: @daniel.watching
Content:
There's a common misconception that the video has fallen into. It's not actually "least action" but "most stable action" as you alluded to at 24:30.

If it was least action, you couldn't have multiple reflections as one reflection is the "least" action. But all locally minimal paths have increased probability too. 

For example, if you have light source with a camera on one side and a mirror on the other, the camera will see the light emitted from the light source and from the reflection, even though the reflected path is twice the distance.

And in theory even a local maxima would have a higher probability. Anywhere where the derivative of the action is close to zero. But how do you have a local maxima for an arbitrary path?

Content:
There is still something fishy with the interpretation of a basketball as a quantum mechanical object. The de Broglie wavelength is smaller than the Planck length for such a massive object. This means that diverging from the path of least action by even a planck length results in a phase change larger than one full period of the de Broglie wavelength which is nonsense because nothing smaller than a planck length makes sense. 

Its important to stress that this is not really physical and its dangerous to believe that an object the size of a basketball has quantum mechanical properties, ie a wavelength that can be attributed to it. There is more to this such as decoherence which plays a major role in the dynamics of macroscopic objects but the suggestion that macroscopic objects such as a basketball have well defined quantum mechanical propoerties such as a de Broglie wavelength lead to all sorts of missconceptions. For example that there is an infinitessimal chance of the basketball tunneling through a wall. No. Just no.

Content:
The problem is assuming from the get go that light behaves like a particle in transit, when it doesn't. It behaves like a wave in transit, a particle upon assignation and interaction. So it doesn't have a "path" at all, at any point. It's a wavefront of potentiality until potential interaction and eventual assignment of the photon. Otherwise, we wouldn't see interference when not monitoring the slits; because to get interference, you have to consider the wave interacting with itself. Particles can't do that.

A physical macro way of imagining it is imagine you have a national temp agency. You might think workers are dispatched from a central location, the HQ, to all job sites around the nation. But what actually happens it that you radio out a broadcast saying "one person go to work somewhere and radio us when you do" and that one person pops up at a job site next door to them and radios you so you broadcast again "we got a guy who went to work, the rest of you don't show up."

There was never a guy dispatched from your HQ who calculated all possible ways to get to the job site.

Author: @DrummerRF
Content:
Small Edit: Just to put it out there. I loved the video and I don't think there is anything said that is wrong except the fact that the final experiment doesn't prove that the "sum of all paths" interpretation is any more predictive than just classical Electrodynamics. Maxwell's equations can also explain all of that. But there is something much more fascinating about the sum of all paths approach that allows you to predict things in QM with Feynman diagrams which is to me really where the magic is. But that is something I don't understand at all. My background is classical electrodynamics in microwaves etc. Not QM at all.

I wanted to give some nuance to the last experiment and what is stated in the video: First of all, I don't think its wrong but its meaning is a bit overstated in my opinion. If someone shines a laser next to my head but not at my eyes I can see the light in the tip of the pointer. The light scatters from the casing etc and goes everywhere. the idea that a laserpointer like the one used in the experiment shoots photons in one direction was wrong to begin with in the sense that its the same as the first lamp but just a more focussed beam. If you truly had a good confined laser you wouldn't see the other paths. But this isn't beause all paths aren't being explored but because the phase shifts are already chaotic for those paths as a function of the geometry and materials of the pointer itself. What you then conclude is that this "all paths exploring"  interpretation is more or less trivial.

In fact, its so trivial that a lot of problems of dynamical systems and physical waves can be seen in this way. In fact you can also formulate a Lagrangian for acoustics which would then imply that there are Phonon particles (virtual) that explore all possible paths where we know that these particals are only mathematical. The point that I would make is that all that is discussed here, while still very interesting, is just that our physical laws can be written in "action like" mathematical statements. To be more precise the entire field of Finite Element simulations that also solve for rigid body deformation problems are founded on the fundamental notion that a set of differential equations that describe the phsyics of a system can be solved by explicitly generating for them a Lagriangian that can be minimized by LInear algebra. The principle of least action is thus more so a mathematical truth simply because we can write Legragians for these dynamical systems. 

Now i'm not enough of an expert at all to know if all well behaved dynamical systems can have a Lagragian, but I do know that dynamical problems that don't even involve particles have some definition of an "Action"  that is minimized. 

To summarize, the whole conclusion of this video is more of a mathematical one: For the differential equations that describe our world, Maxwell's equations, Dirac equation etc, there exists an analogous quantity that we can measure by integrating a Lagrangian that is well chosen that would be minimized only for the solution of those equations. The integral of those legragians then mathematically "look like" infinite path models of particles. Yes this is all true but it isn't in my opinion just equivalent to the underlying equations. I think the true value of this is more so that this mathematical analogy can be leveraged to invent solutions to problems that couldn't be solved by just studying its original form. And perhaps particals do truly go through all possible paths. The problem that I would have is that you can't tell because both models are 1-to-1 the same. Just a different mathematical notation. Instead of solving a differential equation you find the function of which the corresponding Legragian is minimized.

Author: @kirillnovik8661
Content: You can also think of the principle of least action in terms of energy: the path of least action is the one that minimizes the need for extra forces. For a free particle, any deviation from a straight-line path would require an external force, which does work and changes the energy. Similarly, in a constant force field (like gravity), the natural trajectory (e.g., a parabola) follows the force smoothly without needing extra intervention. So in a way, least action can be understood as nature 'choosing' the path that avoids unnecessary energy expenditure

Author: @Linkman81
Content: In the laser experiment at the end of the video, several factors could explain the result. It’s frustrating to see someone confidently claim this proves their point when an observer with less physics knowledge notices something they don’t. He argues that because the laser is visible bouncing off the diffraction grid, even when not pointed at the camera, it supports his claim. However, my point is that the laser behaves like the regular light bulb because the laser isn’t perfect. A truly perfect laser would emit 100% of its light in one direction, making it invisible unless aimed directly at the observer. Yet, we see a red glow around the tip of the laser, indicating scatter or reflection. This glow is visible from any angle, though most of the beam travels straight. Therefore, the laser in this experiment produces the same result as regular light, meaning it does not reinforce his argument since we are seeing scattered light, not the direct beam through the diffraction grid.

Author: @adsadsaddFQ
Content:
Tl dw: yes, light—and in fact, all quantum particles—take all possible paths simultaneously. This idea comes from Feynman's *path integral formulation*, which suggests that a photon (or any quantum particle) explores every possible route from point A to point B. However, these paths interfere with each other, and the ones that contribute most to what we observe are those where the action is minimized—aligning with the classical principle of least time (Fermat's principle).  

This isn’t limited to photons; *all* matter exhibits this behavior at the quantum level. Electrons, atoms, and even large molecules like buckyballs (C₆₀) have been shown to take multiple paths in interference experiments. However, for larger objects, quantum effects become negligible due to *decoherence*—interactions with the environment collapse quantum superpositions into classical behavior. That’s why we don’t see everyday objects, like a baseball, taking multiple paths. But at small enough scales, everything follows this strange quantum rule.

Content:
This whole video is one giant reification fallacy! 🤦‍♂️

Light doesn't "explore all possible paths", and nothing in the video says it would. Light is not a particle, but a wave. The wave goes kinda everywhere, yes, but that doesn't mean all "paths". Particles have paths (in the sense shown in the video), waves don't. E.g., a particle could have a path looping, much like some paths in the video, but a wave couldn't (unless it's deflected).

So, why does anyone think that light is a particle, or even that it has particle-like properties? Because of the characteristics of how the wave is measured. The particleness isn't in the light or its emitter, but in the receptor.

There will be some scatter that makes it into the eclipse shadow.  This is fairly easily explained by further atmospheric scattering.  But there may be a brighter dot at the center of the shadow....I seem to recall this being a thing.....Maybe a video from ~9 years ago that a certain Youtube science communicator made titled "The Brightest Part of a Shadow is in the Middle".

IS this because light is taking all paths as suggested in today's video....or is it an effect of gravity or em interference which makes it veer back back around?

I wanna start by saying I'm not a physicist, but Im a decent thinker and I have learned a lot of physics from physicists and YouTubers with physics degrees.

So there are some inconsistencies here.

First, the only demonstration of the Lagrangian is performed with light. This means we have evidence of action with light only as far as I know from this video.

Secondly, don't just follow formulas! Truly understand what "local" might mean. How else can a thing act on another thing than by acting on it? The answer is in the definition. Local means the "adjacentness" in space of two things. Action therefore becomes how an effect is caused. Therefore, any effect caused is caused by /A/ path of least action, Even if it isn't the path of least action in our specific experiment. For light the prior assumption is classical reflection. If light takes more paths than this classical reflection with incidence and reflection angles matching, we then irrationally say the light is taking paths of more action than the least action which is our classical reflective physics. Instead, isn't this a sign the light is actually travelling along all these paths, and phases cancel out? It sounds like that's what you're saying, but it's not. We have therefore found evidence that subatomic interactions near the reflection surface determinedly reflect the **somethings** in all radial directions, as does the light source emit radially in all directions. Physics seems reticent to just say there are things actually travelling all these paths and actually reflecting like a classical object.

Reflection is really about momentum. Momentum in X and Y directions. For a ball with diagonal momentum in equal parts X and Y momentum and reflecting against a surface, the X direction momentum stays the same, but the Y momentum reverses, from the collision. The surface collision reverses the portion of momentum of the ball that is perpendicular to the surface.

And so what we really should be concluding is that light is made of many tiny particles, all radially emitted from the "light source", and reflecting on atoms against other particles of the same kind (we can assume), by reversing the portion of their momentum perpenducular to some "surface" , and maintaining the portion of their momentum parallel to that surface.

Instead of what we're doing now, and assuming, IRRATIONALY, that simplicity begins with complication... that then **does not** in turn come from simplicity. Much like physicists trying to make "causes come after effects" in some theories, you cannot reinvent the wheel! The definition of a cause is the thing that comes first. Author: @DavidByrden1
Content:
There IS actually something strange about the diagram at 1:50.
To change its vector correctly,  the photon needs to know two things: 
1. The refractive index of the new medium. This is not a problem. The photon is already touching it. The measurement is local.
2. The shape of the boundary. THIS is the weird part. A photon is supposedly very tiny - small enough to be absorbed entirely by a single electron. But, the shape of the boundary cannot be determined over such a small scale; the photon would have to measure over hundreds of atoms, perhaps much further, depending on how rough was the surface. 
Therefore the photon makes a non-local measurement, if it's a particle. But this is all unremarkable - if the photon is a wave.
And that is what the narrator is talking about. In order to behave like a wave, this single photon must take all possible paths, because that's what the wave consists of. But when the photon eventually interacts with something, it will be highly localised, with its entire presence and all of its energy located at a single atom.

Time Travel is the answer. Photons and other particles governed by QM ignore time. Author: @PerfectlyNormalAlex
Content:
Cool video, cool experiment, insane production value as always.
Maybe one criticism: I think it's unhelpful to be talking about paths and probabilities if you want to understand what's really going on. It was a nice crutch to get us from classical thinking, with ideal point particles and well-defined borders, to quantum mechanics, which is way more fuzzy, and it's a really useful computational tool, but it really gives the wrong idea.
A particle, at the quantum level, doesn't just behave like a wave, it IS a wave. It doesn't take paths, in the same way that a water wave doesn't take paths when you dunk a rock in a pond. Every molecule takes a path, but the wave just spreads out as a whole. A physical object is like the wave, not the molecules, it's not made of smaller stuff (not talking about fundamental particles here, just treating it as a quantum object).
In the experiment at the end, the laser light doesn't take different paths to get to the camera, rather it's actually just way more spread out than you think. It exists in the whole room, with varying amplitude. The points you see are just the highest bumps of the wave.

Author: @hedaurabesh
Content:
The experiment with the laser and the slitted foil is interesting, but I wonder whether it is truly showing what it claims to show.
Imagine I replace the foil with a mirror, angled so that the camera can "see" the reflection of the laser's body.

Knowing that no laser can achieve perfect collimation (some light is always scattered and does not go straight), it is no surprise that some red laser light is reflected by the mirror and "seen" by the camera. No exploration of alternate paths required -- just imperfect collimation. And then it makes sense why the reflected laser light is so much weaker than the prime reflection. So treating the slitted foil as an weak reflector works just as well to explain the experiment.

This logic certainly does not show a weakness in quantum theory (the math certainly works out), but it shows a weakness in the experiment, in that it can be explained differently.

Author: @DBHMedia
Content:
When people say a photon “explores all possible paths,” that’s really just a way to describe a math tool we use to predict how light behaves. In reality, light doesn’t literally try every route like a traveler checking every road. Instead, the math sums up all the theoretical paths, and most of them cancel each other out. What remains are the few paths that add together to give the results we observe.

Think of it like a recipe. The math is the recipe that tells us how all the ingredients (or paths) mix together to create the final flavor (or observed behavior). But just because the recipe considers all ingredients doesn’t mean the dish is literally made of every single one. It’s just a way for us to figure out what the final dish should be.

So, while the phrase “explores all paths” might sound like something magical happening in the universe, it’s actually just shorthand for a calculation that helps us make accurate predictions. The photon isn’t doing extra work—it’s simply following the laws of physics, and our math helps us understand why it ends up where it does.

Content:
Everything we see is just constructive interference of matter waves, all following the path of least action. You, me, my hand—everything.

An electron, which is a wave, orbits a nucleus (which itself is a construct of quark waves forming protons/neutrons). This creates a stable pattern we call an atom—for example, hydrogen (one electron + one nucleus). At a certain point in space-time, these waves constructively interfere to appear as particles.

Atoms combine—say, a hydrogen atom bonds with a carbon atom (which has 4 electrons around its nucleus)—forming a C-H bond, again following the least action principle. All organic material? Just a soup of C-H and other bonds, a dance of probability-driven constructive waves.

| Border between quantum & classical |

A collection of these particles = matter. Matter interacts through classical forces like electromagnetism. As matter scales up, we get celestial bodies like the Sun. At this size, new effects emerge—like gravity, becoming observable.

Author: @physicynics-tz2hf
Content: It’s a great video, but with a quite misleading end. The last experiment is diffraction from the laser’s surrounding speckle pattern. That is a phase effect. But some people are thinking you are able to get signal from regions where without it you would measure zero intensity. That is not true though. The action integral is a path integral over, well, the whole path; cancelling out terms at one position doesn’t create amplitude where there was little to start. For that you need to assure coherent phase addition along the entire “indirect” path. You can interpret an optical fiber in that way if you want. It’s important to remember that this is still wave optics/physics, just viewed from a slightly different perspective.

Author: @pablocopello3592
Content:
Christiaan Huygens in S XVII formulated the "Huygens principle" for all waves (each point in a wave front is a source of waves and a new wave front can be found taking the tangent of those "secondary" wavelets). This is "almost" equivalent to the "sum of all paths" formulation, but it is more specific because it establish a way of making the sum (and establish an "implicit" discretization), that avoids the math fundamental problems of "path integral".  So, nothing really NEW with Path Integral, just a vaguely intuitive way of visualizing wave behavior, that is mathematically incorrect and not correctable (without changing some fundamental part of its definition). Path Integral is famous because it avoids to explicitly mention non-locality (but it is essentially non-local in its formulation).
Electron (and other "particles") are NOT like classical particles or classical fields. What we have are "quantum" fields (that have waves), and their main characteristics are that they do not interact with other fields in a continuous way, but in a quantized way (each quantum of interaction is a photon or an electron etc.), and the other (basic) non-classical characteristic is that they are not local (the interaction of the field in some place and time affects the interaction of the same field in other places and times not related by "classical" (space-time propagated) cause-effects).

Author: @timothyp.southwick6542
Content:
Mathematics functions as a type of language that we use to describe and model physical phenomena. In the case of quantum mechanics, the wave function and its collapse is a part of a process of elimination based on probability rather than certainty.
Mathematics is a language method used to describe relationships, structures, and patterns in the natural world and it provides a precise way to express abstract concepts.
The wave function is part of that language, used to represent a system’s state in terms of probabilities. It doesn't tell us the exact outcome but gives us a way to compute the likelihood of each possible outcome.
Process of Elimination in Quantum Mechanics.
Before measurement, a quantum system is of and considered to be in a superposition of multiple states. The wave function mathematically represents this spread-out probability.
When a measurement is made, the wave function collapses to one definite state i.e. eliminating all the other possibilities from the outcome, even though the other possibilities are still considered and thought to exist in a superposed form until measurement.
This is a mathematical process that translates into a physical event where we observe a single result from a range of possibilities.
Wave Function collapse is a system mathematically eliminating all the non-measured states leaving one observable outcome.
The language of mathematics allows us to represent all possible outcomes before measurement and then to describe how one of those outcomes is selected once we interact with the system.
In this way, the mathematical model is a framework for predicting and eliminating possibilities, where each step in the quantum process is defined probabilistically, but ultimately gives a single, observable reality. 
while the mathematics itself is abstract, the process it describes leads to real, observable phenomena that  can be measured and confirmed experimentally.   
Mathematics is a language this is a descriptive tool, not a physical entity.  
The wave function is a mathematical representation of probabilities, not something that physically exists.  
Wave Function Collapse is a process of elimination.
Before measurement, multiple possibilities exist (superposition).  
Measurement eliminates all but one outcome, making the result definite.  
This is not a physical collapse, but a mathematical update of our knowledge.  
Quantum Mechanics is about probabilities, not certainties.  
The wave function is a calculation tool, not a physical wave.  
What we call collapse and is just the removal of unobserved possibilities when we measure.  
The wave function is not a real, physical thing, it is just a mathematical way to describe probabilities.  
There is no physical collapse, only a process of elimination when we make a measurement.  
Quantum mechanics is a probability-based system, not a mysterious physical wave collapsing.

Author: @derhonk6270
Content:
The experiment with the mirror is great, but the laser does not add any meaning to it. You do not see the 'laser beam' in the section with the diffraction grating but the diffuse scattering of light from the aperture of the laser, the same way you saw the other 'normal' lamp before. Theoretically the scattered light from the laser is nothing but a red lamp with a narrow spectrum spreading light in every direction. You can see this is true, because you can see from the side, whether the laser is turned on or off, just by having this scattered light enter your eye, no mirror and no looking into the beam necessary. (If you wanted to double-check in the experiment, cover the aperture of the laser with a small tube around it.)

In this part you just enforce the common misconception that as soon as we involve a laser somewhere, there is nothing but one single straight beam. People seldom wonder, why they can see laser spots, (or see from the side if the laser is running,) if all light from the laser just goes in one straight line that misses your eye.

What a laser could do for your point about light (and other waves) taking every possible path (classically known as the Huygens- or Huygens-Fresnel principle) is trying to explain why a laser beam does not diverge (so much as light from a light bulb) using Gaussian beams. But maybe that leads to far for the general audience outside of physics classes.

In philosophy I came up with a model of time as distance through the state space of the universe, which winds up having lots of implications that resemble the findings of modern physics, from the indeterminism of quantum physics because every state has multiple different future states, through the distortions of space and time of relativistic physics.

But one thing that everyone gets hung up on about it is the implication that every state also has multiple pasts — because surely, they think, there’s definitely only one past that actually happened. To which I bring up Feynman path integrals and say no, actually, they all happened, but they interfere with each other in their effects on the present, so what we see evinced in any given present state is the integral of all the different strings of past states that could have lead there.

And the difference between two states that neighbor each other in the state space, and so equivalently between any consecutive moments of time? That’s h: the quantum of action, the smallest possible change.

Author: @thatchinaboi1
Content:
ChatGPT:  Yes, the claims in the video, while appearing logically consistent within the framework of quantum mechanics, are misleading because they conflate mathematical formalism with ontological reality. Logical consistency is a necessary condition for truth but not a sufficient one—something can be internally consistent yet still be false if its premises are incorrect or its assumptions are unjustified.

Why the Claims Are Misleading, Fallacious, and Erroneous

Mathematical Formalism ≠ Ontological Reality

The video presents Feynman’s path integral formulation as if particles literally explore all possible paths, rather than it being a computational technique.

This is an equivocation fallacy: it treats a mathematical abstraction as if it describes physical reality directly.

Failure to Justify the "All Paths" Interpretation

The claim that particles take every possible path, including superluminal and backward-in-time paths, is presented as a logical necessity.

However, the only justification given is that the math allows for it, which is circular reasoning—assuming what needs to be proven.

The Illusion of Empirical Confirmation

The diffraction grating experiment is used as evidence, but it only demonstrates interference effects, not that light actually travels all possible paths.

This is a non sequitur—jumping to conclusions that do not follow from the premises.

Ambiguous Use of "Least Action"

The claim that least action "emerges" from quantum mechanics contradicts the idea that it is fundamental, yet the video treats both as true.

This is an inconsistency that undermines its own argument.

Logical Consistency and Truth

Logical consistency means a claim does not contradict itself, but it does not guarantee truth. A consistent system can be false if it is based on incorrect or unfounded premises. If these claims were entirely logically consistent—including consistency with ontological reality—then they would indeed be true. However, since they fail to justify their foundational assumptions, they remain erroneous and misleading.

Author: @pyrotas
Content:
This is a typical example of how a wonderful mathematical model, which allows to make some of the most precise predictions, has turned from what it is - a mathematical model - through an interpretation of reality up to “this is why light/matter explores all paths and knows which one to follow”.

Light does not explore a thing. Classically, a plane wave (and its associated ray) follows deterministic local rules dictated by Maxwell’s equations that precisely predict not only how wave fronts bend, but also how polarization changes (something that path integrals ignore). Same goes for quantum mechanics. Don’t get me wrong: stationary action principles are some of the most elegant and powerful ways to formulate and solve mathematical models in theoretical physics and are here to stay unchallenged until we invent something even better - classically, relativistically, quantum or in any combination thereof. But they remain mathematical constructs. “Nature behaves AS IF” is not the same as “nature DOES what that maths tells about”. 

This is an all too common misconception about variational approaches: they make for very compelling and pictorially attractive stories. Which are not necessarily “how Nature works”.

Content: I have heard this described as everything is possible, but not everything is probable. I believe Schrödinger's point was in reference to this, as he said we can't compare events (actions) at a quantum scale to things at a macro scale. Reality begins to break down so his rebuttal holds as scale increases. Likewise people often overstate the idea of probability guiding things without regard for organization that happens at scale and treat reality as being purely unpredictable. The intersection of both is where we don't really educate people. For example, a person is a highly organized entity at the macro scale as a "whole" object, but we are made of enough small interactions and interact with enough entities at a small scale (radiation, molecules, etc), that improbable things seem to happen to people, like getting rare diseases or cancers. It's the inability of the human mind to treat both the improbable and possible as being equally important in determining outcomes. It seems contradictory only through our lack of comprehension across the vast spectrum of possibilities at different scales. Our brains just aren't well designed to predict outcomes at scales outside of our common frame of reference.

Content:
The Quantum Path Resonance Theory
The Quantum Path Resonance Theory proposes that consciousness itself operates according to principles similar to those governing quantum particles. Just as quantum particles explore all possible paths simultaneously with their probability distributions determined by constructive and destructive interference, human decision-making and thought processes may operate according to a similar mechanism on a neural level.
Core Concepts

Neural Action Minimization: Similar to how particles follow paths that minimize action, neural pathways that require the least energetic expenditure become preferentially reinforced through repeated use. However, unlike classical particles, neural pathways maintain a quantum-like superposition of potential routes.
Thought-Path Exploration: When faced with a decision or problem, the conscious mind doesn't actually evaluate one option at a time sequentially. Instead, it explores all possible thought paths simultaneously across parallel neural networks, with most paths destructively interfering and canceling out.
Consciousness Diffraction: Just as light can be diffracted to reveal alternative paths, certain mental states (meditation, psychedelics, or near-death experiences) could act as "consciousness diffraction gratings" that temporarily reveal thought paths normally canceled by destructive interference.
Decision Action Constant: The theory proposes a fundamental constant (similar to Planck's constant) that governs the threshold at which neural activity collapses from a superposition of potential thoughts into a single conscious decision.

Implications
If confirmed, this theory would suggest that intuition, creative insights, and even synchronicities are actually manifestations of temporary access to normally canceled thought-paths. It would explain why humans sometimes arrive at solutions without conscious reasoning and why certain altered states of consciousness appear to expand subjective perception.
The theory also suggests that technologies could potentially be developed to "diffract" consciousness deliberately, allowing access to thought paths that would normally destructively interfere, potentially unlocking untapped creative and problem-solving capabilities within the human mind.
While completely speculative and not supported by current neuroscience, this theory represents an intriguing application of quantum path principles to the realm of consciousness and cognition.

Author: @PartialPsycho
Content:
Looking at the laser and slit film experiment.  How is energy conserved if photons can be destructively interfered by nearby paths, but the interference can be stopped by slits?  Since we can only measure the energy of photons that  hit our detector, we can't measure photons that are removed from existence by destructive interference.

Or, to put it another way.  If we had identical sensors (to the atom) arranged in a sphere, each the same distance down to the Planck length from a point in space, and at that point, a photon is emitted. Assuming the only things in the universe are the detectors and the photon (no other electromagnetic or gravitational waves), would each detector measure a photon?  Since light travels all possible paths, and each detector is the same path in this thought experiment, they should each measure a photon as the light wave propagates outward. But light travels as a discrete package of energy, so we would measure as many photons as we had detectors so energy isn't conserved.

Author: @willmaher8430
Content:
The universe is fundamentally probabilistic, not deterministic. At the quantum level, particles exist in a range of possible states, and their behavior follows probability rather than strict causality. As more particles interact in larger systems, the probability of them following the most stable, expected path increases, making macroscopic objects appear deterministic. However, this determinism is an illusion of scale—unlikely outcomes still remain possible, just increasingly improbable. The universe does not follow a single fixed path but instead overwhelmingly favors the most probable outcomes.

My thoughts:

This probabilistic nature of reality has implications for free will. If the future is not fully determined, then human decisions are not entirely preordained either. While many choices follow habitual, near-deterministic patterns, at key moments, multiple possibilities may exist without a predetermined answer. Because we can reflect on our choices, consider ethical frameworks, and shape our identity over time, free will emerges—not as absolute independence from causality, but as the ability to navigate real, open-ended decisions within a probabilistic universe. In this way, human choice is neither purely random nor entirely determined, but a process of self-definition in the face of uncertainty.

Author: @drakedbz
Content:
My problem with the example shown is that the diffraction grating isn't infinitely thin, and the edge between gap and not-gap in the grating is not infinitely sharp. If there is even a slight curve, light can hit at the proper angle of incidence to reach the camera. Think of it like shining light off of jail cell bars (a massively scaled up version of the diffraction grating). Also, the problem with actual physical implementations of lasers is that they aren't perfect. You can see that light is being emitted from the end, even if they are not pointing directly at you because some amount of light is being sent your direction, presumably from diffraction/reflection in relation to the materials that make the end of the laser device. Until those two problems can be solved experimentally (which as far as I'm aware, all physical objects will run into the first problem, since they would be made of atoms, which have a physical size), it's not possible to 100% prove the theory mentioned with the shown experiment.

Now, all of that said, I'm fully aware that we understand all particles to act as waves (this is high school physics), but even if that's the case, it's entirely irrelevant for objects meaningfully larger than an atom. I would be very surprised if there were a practical application for that effect, specifically in regards to larger objects acting that way.

Author: @savagefoox3524
Content:
I love your videos and this is interesting, but I think this is an example of the construct of math interfering with the discovery of truth in science. In the end, common sense rules out the possibility that something travels infinite possible ways every time it moves. That’s preposterous. Everything about logic screams in your mind that this is not true. This is mathematics which is a construct in itself, trying to make sense of something. It doesn’t know how to make sense of and humans, forcing an answer. This happens too often in science. Additionally, if we use this messy mathematical approach to try to make it un-messy, common sense tells us that we should see the light distributed evenly across the entire surface through however, many slips you have and not forming lights. If light can travel in all possible directions, and if we’re suggesting that light explores all possible directions than this mathematical conundrum still does not explain why ends up where it ends up after passing through the slit. Clearly there is a correlation between where the light is aimed and where it ends up. There’s a physical element to it does not include infinite possibilities. It also leaves a bad taste in your mouth when you end up with this conclusion that we know intuitively and logically through common sense that it’s not the case just because we can twist mathematics to make it work. We know that it’s not true. The two slit experiment doesn’t travel forward and backwards in time. when we get in our car and drive to school to drop off our kids, it’s not an arbitrary thing, and the headlights in our car are not arbitrarily lighting up the road instead of lighting up the forest on some other planet in the future. It’s too easy to get caught up in these thought experiments and then come out with a conclusion. That sounds really cool but is preposterous. This is the same kind of mistake that the cart made I think therefore I am. No… You are therefore you think or more precisely you are therefore you’re being makes it possible that you might think if you’re capable of thought but being proceeds thought not thought proceeds being. So my point is that you can make this mathematical conundrum result in an answer by forcing it, and you might touch on some kind of pattern recognition within reality that leads you to a result that makes you think like your finding some truth and perhaps you are finding truth, but you’re not finding definitive answer, and this is what philosophy tells us. Philosophically This explanation can’t follow. Light cannot travel from .8 to point B in an infinite number of ways. It’s direction is determined by the physical light source and the direction the photos are being admitted, and it concludes some possibilities because the light can’t both go forward and backwards in the direction where it’s not being projected. So you can’t apply an infinity of possibilities for its movement from .8 to point B just because you manipulate the math to make that work. Math cannot be the ultimate proof of reality. Math can sometimes come up with an answer that can predict reality to some degree of accuracy and it is very very useful in doing so but math does not define or generate reality. Reality defines math. So when you try to use math to define reality, you always have to respect the fact that you might discover something true about reality using the tool of mathematics, but you cannot use the tool of mathematics to actually define reality. Do you see the distinction? Reality defines what’s possible for mathematics to discover and mathematics is not perfect. There’s 1 million examples of why math is not perfect. The problem of zero. Using base 10 as opposed to base 12 or base 20 or base 30. They have uses but every single Mathematical construct that we try to use has limitations. And sure we hope for a unified theory of everything, but that presupposes a mathematical system that is perfectly unified and we definitely haven’t discovered that. We don’t even know if it can be discovered because it may just be the case that math is Ultimately an imperfect tool that is incapable of producing a unified, perfect truth.
Thank you very much again for the video. It’s fun to think about these things. I find myself watching a lot of your videos because their thought provoking and entertaining and while this video was more theoretical and esoteric, you’ve got so many videos that are entertaining that do fun things I really appreciate it and I know my kids enjoy them as well so keep up the wonderful content and I’m sure I’ll enjoy another one of your videos soon.

Content:
If the Laser was better shielded to block the unfocused light, I doubt the refraction sheet would show anything.
The Laser used in the demonstration at the end did not show anything new that the light did not. The light caught by the diffraction sheet was not the intense focused laser light, but the low intensity unfocused light leaking out the front of the laser pointer (Just like you can see when he holds the laser pointer to the side at 29:48, it's not the focused laser pointing at the camera)
The intensity of the light on the diffraction sheet would have to drastically increase when the laser points at the appropriate reflection point to reflect at the camera (without the diffraction sheet) for this to be significant.

If he was to shine the laser directly at the diffraction sheet, it would be interesting to see what pattern the reflected light would make and he could use this to get a (somewhat) focused beam to hit the camera, but it just ends up being a 2-layer many slits experiment and doesn't really tell anything more than those experiments.

Content:
Feynman explains this in his lecture A Quantum Mechanical View of Reality. I HIGHLY recommend watching Angela Collier's video on Feynman, but the one thing he was especially good at, as she acknowledges, is lecturing. And that lecture is recorded and available on YouTube.

In it, he explains this concept to a continuing education class, so people knowledgeable but not professional in physics from the time, which means a lot of them were primed to be skeptical of quantum mechanics.

One student says that if Feynman were correct, then if you remove parts of a mirror, it would reflect better than a whole mirror. Feynamn replies that not only is that correct, but the experiment has been done and that is exactly what happens. But you have to carefully remove only negative interference sections of the mirror. It's a pretty precise experiment to get it to work.

Edit: the clip you showed of Feynman is from that lecture when he explains this experiment.

Author: @kiraPh1234k
Content:
A big issue I have with this is your use of light as an analogy. 

So, first you mentioned "light, and by extension everything" -- No. That's not how that works, light is demonstrably a wave. Not a particle, not a wave-particle, not wave-like, it's a wave. Specifically a wave in the electromagnetic field. 
The idea of a photon comes purely from its interactions with quantum particles, where such interactions are restricted by quanta. 
It does not follow that what happens with light just happen to other things, especially things we tend to regard as particles or under the particle-wave duality. 

As well, I would actually argue that is hasn't been sufficiently demonstrated that there is such a duality in all particles and that some experiments preemptively confirmed a biased interpretation of what is happening. 

Take for example doing double slit with electrons: even if the electron is purely a particle, it's movement through space creates electromagnetic waves, these waves in turn affect the movement of electrons, including the electron that made them. 
This, while similar to light in that it's affected by interference in the waves in that field is also significantly different from light which itself is purely a wave in that field.

The point about all paths existing is perfectly correct since the integral of all possible paths is why these sidebands exist.

I like Feynman’s QED book so much that I kept a stack of them to give to people. You covered it well.

Author: @ViTALMaTThews
Content:
Ok, but no. This only works for light because there are trillions upon trillions of particles being emitted. You are measuring probability and thus some photons will not align with the main beam of light, even in a laser. The same principal can be measured by determining the probability of an electron near the positive part of an atom: the electron will take all possible paths around its orbit of the positive center and the only way you can measure its location is by making the electron cloud the probability of where the electron may be in association with the nucleus. The electron could theoretically be on the surface of the sun, but probabilistically this is beyond zero because that’s stupid. 

Saying that everything in the world, including a basketball, takes all possible paths before reaching a destination is missing the mark of what is being discussed by the experiment. Photons are not sentient and behave like classical mechanics individually (much like a basketball in classical mechanics) but as a group with trillions of incredibly small particles, then there is no way to isolate the measurement of a single photon or electron so you must use probability. Photons, electrons, and even smaller elementary particles such as leptons and quarks, are not sentient and do not “seek out” every path in existence. There are trillions of outcomes and thus you must measure based upon probability. The beam of light is the most probable outcome and thus the majority of photons follow that path. If you could measure one single photo, it would behave just like a basketball, but that would be impossible to measure because the photon literally interacts with trillions of electrons, photons, and elementary particles on its course of being measured. 

The idea that a particle can be in two places at once is a misnomer and asinine. The whole point of the shrodingers dilemma is that you cannot guess the path of a photon or particle because it is impossible to know until you measure it. The whole basis of quantum mechanics is that the particles are so small, that probabilistically the particle is in two places at once, not that it is actually in two places. 

Expressing all of everything as behaving like classical mechanics is wrong.

Content:
Good episode!
Roughly 3-7 times per week I question Claude or another AI about the double-slit experiment because there are some bits that still don't make sense to me, to be honest. 
I was super excited to hear the assertion that everything has a wavelength because I made the guess that this was true in casual conversation at work back in 2015 and was mocked horribly for it (manufacturing job with sewing machines, and no, I am not well-liked).

Now, there is a consequence to this idea that we ought to have been able to demonstrate with the laser. Rather than restrict the foil to the plane of the mirror, Casper might have explored the more ridiculous pathways light might take. If, for example, had it been demonstrated that photons emitted from the laser ended up behind the laser, I would have taken a walk around the block with my hands clasped behind my bowed back with brows furrowed in stern concentration as I stared at the sidewalk passing under my feet, but with my vision of the exterior world occluded by diagrams of potential paths of particles in my mind's eye. As it stands, the results given didn't seem all that surprising.
I want to thank you for showing how we came to the conclusion that light travels in discrete packets. In the back of my mind, I believe there is room for the impossible infinite-energy light beam when the amplitudes approach zero because so much else is insane in physics, so why not? 
There are consequences to this business of all things exploring all possible trajectories and arriving at the ones where there is least destructive interference regarding thought, consciousness, and free will. I realize that sort of talk normally lands outside of your scope, but gosh darn it would I enjoy a Veritasium take on some philosophical topics. Here's why I find it interesting: When we go about our everyday experiences, we see our choices as those which naturally might occur, with some deviations entering the picture now and then.

One last thing — I'm seeing for the first time that Veritasium has the same atomic weight as a weird unstable isotope of calcium courtesy of Douglas Adams, and in November it became your age. I just found that funny. Truly, we are in the age of Veritasium and ought not to panic and bring a towel.

If a particle in the double-slit experiment explores all possible paths, some of those paths would be infinitely long—like circular paths or those that would take multiple times the age of the universe to traverse, even at the speed of light (or beyond, if superluminal exploration were possible). This raises a deeper question about the physical mechanism underlying this exploration. If we don’t fully understand it, paradoxes like this naturally emerge.

Author: @MaulikParmar210
Content:
The multiple path assumptions come from ignoring the quantized state, as the causality happens and the observer observes the particle, it takes a form and collapses super position, that's pretty simple quantum mechanics happening right in front of our eyes and gets ignored in almost all the thought experiments. 

Superposition is a snapshot of the state of any system, it's not suppose to tell you other dimensions that affects whatever is going to happen next. The moment you're observing and deciding these dimensions, the superposition collapses to a single truth wrt. observer's PoV. So no it actually doesn't have infinite physical paths, but infinite possibilities that can happen, it only has to choose one depending on the context it's being observed.

Mach–Zehnder interferometer  experiment is better at explaining the probability aspects of the quantum mechanics happening with photons. We often ignore time as a dimension in these experiments while explaining, and we observe single photon, but irl there are multiple photons and time involved to observe the experiment, which is not usually accounted for explaining why we cannot traceback the path without destroying superposition state.  TEM lasers may allow you to determine where photon came from, but then you have already manipulated it to decide it's fate. It's all about possibilities in point in time, the moment time flows, quantum collapses.
